title: A Machine Learning Model Based on Ultrasound Radiomics and Multi-modal Clinical Features for Predicting Lymph Node Metastasis of Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma in the Setting of Hashimoto's Thyroiditis.
abstract: Objective To investigate the value of multi-modal features (ultrasound characteristics, BRAF V600E mutation, and TPO-Ab) in predicting lymph node metastasis (LNM) of papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) in the context of Hashimoto's thyroiditis (HT), and to construct machine learning models for individualized risk assessment. Methods A retrospective cohort of 377 patients with pathologically confirmed PTC and concurrent HT was enrolled and divided into LNM n=186 and non-LNM n=191 groups. Preoperative ultrasound features (e.g., Minimum Tumor-to-Capsule Distance (DTC_min), calcification type and ratio, lesion location, nodule morphology), serological and pathological indicators were collected. Random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost and XGB), logistic regression (LR), and k-nearest neighbors (KNN) were used to build prediction models. Feature importance was assessed, and model performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and calibration curves. Results Univariate analysis showed that calcification type, nodule diameter, DTC_min, and aspect ratio were significantly associated with LNM, with nodule diameter contributing the most. Overall, the integration of multi‑omics features significantly improved the accuracy of lymph node metastasis prediction. Radiomics features contributed the largest share (81.5%), followed by morphological features (M1: DTC_min/Size/Calcification, 12.7%), while molecular markers and genetic biomarkers provided supplementary information (M2: TPO‑Ab, 3.8%; M3: BRAF V600E, 2.0%). Notably, the optimal XGBoost model achieved a stable accuracy of 0.879 in an independent external cohort (n = 107), confirming its robust generalizability for clinical risk assessment. Conclusion In the HT setting, machine learning models based on multi-omics feature fusion enable effective individualized risk stratification for PTC LNM, offering precise support for clinical decision-making.

title: Automatic Multiparametric Quantitative Ultrasound Framework for Segmentation and Characterization of Layered Soft Tissues.
abstract: To diagnose diseases associated with changes in body composition, such as sarcopenia or muscle wasting due to cancer, it is necessary to accurately evaluate muscle and fat layers. However, conventional B-mode ultrasound has limitations due to its high dependence on the ultrasound examiner and subjective interpretation. In this study, we propose a multiparametric quantitative ultrasound (QUS) framework that automatically detects tissue boundaries and segments laminar tissues by combining attenuation images estimated using the Regularized Spectral Log Difference (RSLD) method with midband fit, spectral intercepts, Nakagami images and echogenicity mapping. Boundaries were identified through 2-D connectivity component analysis on the integrated QUS map, which allowed for the detection of discontinuous or stepped boundaries without assuming lateral continuity, followed by refinement using a Chan-Vese active contour model. This framework was evaluated using a homogeneous reference phantom, a customized lateral heterogeneous staircase phantom, and an ex vivo swine shoulder specimen. The results of the staircase phantom experiment showed that the segmented block thickness matched actual physical measurements within 2.3%-5.0% across all four regions, despite the stepped boundary geometry. In ex vivo experiments, the estimated fat and muscle thicknesses also matched actual measurements within 4.8% and 1.3%, respectively, and fat and muscle regions showed distinct QUS parameter values. These preliminary results support the feasibility of automatically characterizing tissue characteristics by combining multiple QUS parameters into a single integrated segmentation framework, and lay the groundwork for further validation studies using diverse samples for future body composition assessment.

title: Evaluation of Pulse Repetition Frequency in Laminectomy-Free Transvertebral Blood-Spinal Cord Barrier Opening Using Low-Intensity Focused Ultrasound: A Parameter Screening Study in Rats.
abstract: Objective The blood-spinal cord barrier (BSCB) serves as a critical structure that maintains the homeostasis of the spinal cord microenvironment. However, its highly selective permeability restricts the entry of macromolecular therapeutic agents into the spinal parenchyma. Although low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) combined with microbubbles has been reported to transiently open the BSCB, the impact of specific exposure parameters requires further investigation. In this study, we evaluated the pulse repetition frequency (PRF)/duty cycle regimens of LIFU in a laminectomy-free rat model and examined the acute histologic outcomes and behavioral performance. Methods In this study, BSCB opening by LIFU and microbubbles was evaluated in rats without performing laminectomy. We compared PRFs ranging from 1 to 10 Hz. The efficacy of BSCB opening was quantitatively assessed by calculating the percentage of Evans Blue dye extravasation area per unit area from fluorescence microscopy images, and the degree of tissue damage was systematically compared. Subsequently, we evaluated selected regimens and monitored functional outcomes under the candidate 1-Hz PRF/2% duty cycle protocol over a 28-day observation period. Results Our results demonstrated that the 1-Hz PRF/2% duty cycle protocol (total duration, 300 s; burst-on acoustic power, 3 W; peak negative pressure, 0.984 MPa; 20-ms burst length) effectively opened the BSCB without causing statistically significant acute tissue damage. Furthermore, no overt sensory or motor deficits were observed during the 28-day evaluation. Conclusion This study demonstrated a well-tolerated and laminectomy-free BSCB opening protocol through the screening of PRF/duty cycle regimens, offering a promising avenue for the targeted delivery of macromolecules to the spinal cord.

title: Endourological Surgery in Low-Middle Income Countries in Africa: A Needs-Assessment Survey of Infrastructure, Equipment, Disposables, and Barriers to Care.
abstract: Objective To characterize and quantify barriers to endoscopic urologic procedures across low- and middle-income countries with a needs-assessment survey of urologic facilities, equipment, disposable usage, and procedures currently being performed. We queried urologists on the perceived barriers to performing more complex endourological procedures to better direct international improvement efforts. Methods A 30-item survey assessing facility characteristics, infrastructure, equipment, disposable supplies, and procedural barriers was distributed to endourologists at an international conference. Responses were stratified into low-income (LIC) and middle-income (MIC) groups based on World Bank classifications. Responses were summarized as frequencies and percentages. Results Among 109 respondents (56 LIC, 53 MIC), basic hospital infrastructure was generally available, but major critical gaps existed for advanced imaging and intraoperative resources. No access to laser fibers was reported by 74% of LIC and 46% of MIC respondents. Among urologists with access, reuse of disposable fibers until failure was common (86% LIC, 31% MIC). Flexible ureteroscopy was available for 56% of respondents, with limited scope availability as the primary barrier. PCNL was available for 46% of respondents, with insufficient surgical training the most cited barrier. Intraoperative ultrasound was more available than fluoroscopy. Conclusion Equipment supply chains and procedure-specific infrastructure, more than surgical training and hospital infrastructure, were major barriers to advanced endourologic care in LMICs. Structured needs-assessments of endourologic capacity provide a framework for targeted collaboration. Volunteer workshops should involve local stakeholders, be procedure-specific, and data-driven to provide appropriate support.

title: Molecular profiling of renal mass biopsy tissue: A review of feasibility and clinical utility.
abstract: Conventional preoperative assessment of renal masses may not fully capture biologic aggressiveness, particularly for small or indeterminate lesions where reliance on imaging, histopathology, and tumor size can limit individualized risk assessment. As molecular classification becomes increasingly utilized in renal tumor diagnosis, renal mass biopsy (RMB) tissue provides an opportunity to preoperatively address this gap to support patient-specific management. We reviewed the feasibility and potential clinical relevance of molecular profiling performed on RMB tissue. PubMed and Embase were searched for English-language human studies published from January 1, 2010, to February 19, 2026. Eligible studies included adults with primary renal masses who underwent genomic, transcriptomic, or proteomic analysis of biopsy-derived solid tissue. Findings were synthesized descriptively by profiling modality, technical feasibility, molecular findings, reported diagnostic, prognostic, or management implications. Exploratory quantitative synthesis was performed for studies with extractable technical-feasibility denominators. Thirteen studies were included, evaluating DNA-based, RNA-based/transcriptomic, and proteomic or multi-omic profiling approaches. Nine studies with extractable technical feasibility or tissue adequacy outcomes reported high observed approach-specific success rates: DNA-based 97% (482/496), RNA-based 100% (254/254), and proteomic/multi-omic 100% (22/22). Biopsy-derived profiling identified molecular features relevant to benign-malignant discrimination, subtype refinement, small renal mass risk stratification, and characterization of biologic programs associated with aggressive tumor behavior. Molecular profiling of RMB tissue appears feasible and may provide biologically meaningful information beyond imaging and histopathology. Prospective studies using standardized preoperative RMB workflows are needed to determine whether biopsy-derived profiling improves risk stratification and supports precision management.

title: Evaluation of serological changes of ESR, CRP, IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-a) and hematologic parameters in pet dogs with pyometra.
abstract: Canine pyometra is associated with systemic inflammation, but erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) has been less extensively evaluated alongside cytokines, C-reactive protein (CRP), and routine hematologic variables. This case-control study compared inflammatory and hematologic measurements in 15 dogs with closed pyometra and 15 clinically healthy controls. Interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), CRP, ESR, white blood cell (WBC) count, packed cell volume (PCV), and serum creatinine were assessed. Group differences were analyzed using independent-samples t-tests, with Welch correction when variance heterogeneity was detected. Mean differences were reported with 95% confidence intervals and Hedges' g effect sizes. Dogs with closed pyometra had higher IL-6, TNF-α, CRP, ESR, and WBC counts and lower PCV and serum creatinine than controls (all p ≤ 0.005). The largest standardized differences were observed for ESR (g = 2.39), PCV (g = -2.29), and serum creatinine (g = -1.94). Within the pyometra group, IL-6, TNF-α, and CRP were strongly correlated (r = 0.974-0.978; p < 0.001). These findings demonstrate a pronounced systemic inflammatory and hematologic phenotype in closed canine pyometra and identify ESR as a potentially informative component of multimarker inflammatory assessment. Prospective studies incorporating longitudinal measurements and clinical outcomes are required to determine diagnostic or prognostic utility.

title: Titanium miniplate fixation of complex carapacial and plastral fractures in a young red-footed tortoise (Chelonoidis carbonarius): A case report with three-year follow-up.
abstract: Background Traumatic shell fractures in chelonians may involve the carapace, plastron, and underlying osseous structures, resulting in mechanical instability and potentially severe associated injuries. Although several shell repair techniques have been described, information regarding rigid titanium plate fixation and its long-term outcome in growing red-footed tortoises ( Chelonoidis carbonarius ) is limited. Case presentation A young, growing red-footed tortoise ( C. carbonarius ) of unknown age and weighing approximately 400 g was presented one day after accidental vehicular trauma with complex fractures involving both the carapace and plastron. Clinical and radiographic assessment demonstrated substantial displacement and mechanical instability. Surgical stabilization was performed using titanium straight and reconstruction miniplates, which were sectioned and contoured intraoperatively to conform to the three-dimensional geometry of the shell. Immediate postoperative radiography documented fracture reduction and implant positioning. At approximately one year after surgery, clinical follow-up demonstrated maintenance of shell integrity, substantial continued growth, and persistence of the fixation implants. During the subsequent follow-up period, the owner reported progressive loss of some plate segments as the tortoise contacted the implants against objects and obstacles within its enclosure, without reported clinical complications. At approximately three years, substantial additional shell growth was evident, with one reconstruction plate segment remaining in place and a localized alteration in shell contour adjacent to the region of the retained hardware. Long-term radiographic follow-up was unavailable; therefore, a causal relationship between the retained implant and the contour alteration could not be established. Conclusion Contoured titanium miniplates provided rigid stabilization of complex carapacial and plastral fractures in this young red-footed tortoise. The three-year clinical outcome supports the feasibility of this fixation strategy while highlighting the importance of long-term monitoring and reassessment of retained rigid implants in actively growing chelonians.

title: Central nervous system involvement, sequelae, and prognostic markers in children with severe hand-foot-and-mouth disease: A multicenter cohort study across four Chinese cities.
abstract: Approximately 10% of severe hand-foot-mouth disease (HFMD) cases develop post-recovery sequelae such as language and cognitive impairments, posing major social and family burdens. However, large-scale evidence on long-term outcomes is limited. This multicenter cohort study retrospectively analyzed hospitalized HFMD cases between January 1, 2015, and December 31, 2023, in four cities (Zhengzhou, Changchun, Xi'an, and Zhoukou). Among 25,536 medical records, all severe HFMD inpatients were identified, and mild HFMD inpatients from the same period were randomly selected as controls at a 1:1 ratio, resulting in 1,909 patients in each group. Sequelae were assessed through long-term follow-up, and potential prognostic markers were examined using Kaplan-Meier survival analysis and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models. The result showed that severe HFMD was associated with a significantly higher risk of long-term sequelae compared with mild cases, including motor disorders, epilepsy, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, tic disorders, language disorders, developmental delays, psychiatric disorders, intellectual disabilities, and social impairments. Independent predictors of sequelae were peak fever, feeding mode, serum creatinine, serum sodium, and complement C3 levels, which together provided effective prediction of the 6-year cumulative risk. Abnormal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and electroencephalography (EEG) findings during the acute phase were strongly correlated with subsequent sequelae. Furthermore, learning disabilities were more common among patients with severe HFMD, further highlighting the potential long-term neurological and neurodevelopmental burden of the disease. Together, these findings underscore the importance of long-term follow-up and further research to improve early identification of children at risk and inform strategies to reduce the long-term effect of HFMD.

title: Awake Craniotomy for Eloquent and Near-Eloquent Brain Tumors Without MRI or Intraoperative Neuromonitoring During the Gaza War: A Six-Patient Case Series.
abstract: Objective To describe patient selection, intraoperative neurological assessment, and postoperative observations in six awake brain tumor resections performed without MRI or electrical stimulation mapping during the Gaza war. Methods We reviewed six awake procedures undertaken at two Gaza neurosurgical services between February 2025 and July 2026. CT guided anatomical planning; patients remained awake with scalp block, local infiltration, and anesthesiologist-supervised sedation. The operating surgeon performed motor or language assessment appropriate to the lesion location. Operative records, available CT descriptions, and subsequent clinical clarifications informed the analysis. Results Among 125 tumor craniotomies reported by the participating services, six were performed awake; the number eligible for awake surgery was not recorded. All six procedures were completed without conversion to general anesthesia or a reported intraoperative clinical functional change. Five resections were judged complete by the surgeon and one intentionally subtotal, without MRI-based volumetric verification. One patient developed postoperative right hemiplegia with only partial improvement reported about one week later and died three months after surgery. The five other patients had reported follow-up of 1-18 months (median, 9 months). CT lesion dimensions were supplied for all cases, but source imaging was not independently re-reviewed. The surgeon recalled operative durations of approximately two to three hours. Conclusions Awake clinical examination provided limited real-time functional feedback when standard mapping tools were unavailable. These observations do not establish comparative safety, complete resection, or equivalence to stimulation mapping. Their relevance lies in the operative choices, limitations, and postoperative morbidity documented under resource constraints.

title: Direct Revascularization for Moyamoya Disease: Intraoperative Anastomotic Thrombus Formation With Preoperative Aspirin and an Atraumatic Microsurgical Technique.
abstract: Background Intraoperative anastomotic thrombus formation during direct revascularization for moyamoya disease (MMD) may compromise bypass patency. This study describes the procedural outcomes and safety of a contemporary strategy combining refined atraumatic microsurgical technique with standardized preoperative aspirin. Methods We retrospectively reviewed 168 hemispheres that underwent combined direct and indirect revascularization for MMD between 2018 and 2025. The primary cohort comprised 115 hemispheres treated by a single surgeon with this strategy; aspirin was withheld for 2 days before surgery and resumed on postoperative day 1. Primary outcomes were intraoperative anastomotic thrombus formation, thrombus-related reanastomosis, and bypass patency; perioperative ischemic and hemorrhagic complications were also recorded. Data from an earlier cohort treated with a different technique without aspirin are presented descriptively. Results In the primary cohort, thrombus formation occurred in 3 of 115 anastomoses (2.6%; 95% confidence interval, 0.5%-7.4%), and 1 (0.9%) required reanastomosis. Magnetic resonance angiography confirmed patency of all direct bypasses. No symptomatic ischemic complications occurred. Symptomatic hyperperfusion-related intracerebral hemorrhage occurred in 1 hemisphere (0.9%). In the earlier cohort, thrombus formation occurred in 23 of 106 anastomoses (22%); because the cohorts differed in surgeon, technique, number of anastomoses, era, and age, this difference cannot be attributed to aspirin. Conclusions A combined strategy of refined atraumatic microsurgical technique and preoperative aspirin was associated with a low incidence of intraoperative anastomotic thrombus formation and consistent bypass patency. The independent contribution of aspirin cannot be determined from this study and requires prospective evaluation with systematic platelet function testing.

title: Adaptive Replanning in Hypofractionated Stereotactic Radiosurgery for Large Brain Metastases.
abstract: Background In hypofractionated stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS), adaptive replanning can account for dynamic tumor changes occurring during treatment; however, its clinical relevance remains unclear. We retrospectively evaluated 103 large brain metastases (BMs) (>7 cc) from 86 patients treated with hypofractionated Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS). Methods We assessed inter-fractional tumor volume changes using stereotactic computed tomography obtained after the third fraction, with a ≥10% decrease used as the operational threshold for replanning. Of 103 lesions, 42 (41%) demonstrated inter-fractional tumor volume reduction of ≥10% and underwent adaptive replanning with target volume reduction. No lesion exhibited a significant volume increase. Results Adaptive replanning was not associated with the increased rates of radiation necrosis (4.8% vs. 8.2%) or transient swelling (36% vs. 34%), and no significant differences were observed between the groups for local tumor control or overall survival. In exploratory multivariable Cox regression, inter-fractional tumor volume reduction was associated with improved 1-year local tumor control (hazard ratio per 1% decrease, 0.91; 95% confidence interval, 0.84-0.99; p = 0.031). Conclusions Adaptive replanning based on early volumetric response was feasible during hypofractionated SRS for large BMs and was not associated with increased toxicity; however, a clinical benefit of replanning over non-adaptive treatment, including a reduction in radiation necrosis or transient swelling, was not demonstrated. Inter-fractional tumor volume reduction may serve as an early indicator of favorable local control.

title: Development and In-Vitro Validation of the First Functional, Patient Specific, Metal Additively Manufactured Aneurysm Clip.
abstract: Objective Recent aneurysm clip improvements enhance biocompatibility and imaging artifacts through new materials, while design remained limited. This study aimed to investigate the feasibility of 3D printing aneurysm clips, including the development of the first functional, patient-specific, metal 3D-printed clip. Methods A 5.8 mm wide case of unruptured intracranial aneurysm previously treated with aneurysm ligation through clipping was included, and a complete imaging dataset acquired and segmented. One standard and one patient-specific clip design were evaluated using a Finite Element Model (FEM) simulation to assess clip blade dimensions with respect to the aneurysm sac. Metal 3D printing was employed to produce the clip blades, then assembled with standard clip springs. The produced prototypes were then tested on a silicone 3D-printed physical simulator under exoscope visualization and indocyanine green angiography in a neurosurgical laboratory. Occlusion of the implanted patient-specific clip was then assessed using CT imaging. Results The FEM simulations confirmed design adequacy, with the patient-specific design reducing maximum strain and stress than the standard design respectively of 4.3% and 14%. Both 3D-printed clip designs presented self-occluding functionality, with a maximum dimensional deviation of 90 μm, and a tip-to-tip aperture capacity reduced from 9 mm of traditional clips to 7 mm and 6 mm, respectively. The 3D-printed clips fully occluded the silicone aneurysm sac. The patient-specific design avoided dog-ear formation and improved vascular reconstruction, then radiologically confirmed. Conclusions Metal 3D printing enabled the first self-closing, patient-specific aneurysm clip, with functional feasibility demonstrated in a simulated setting; comprehensive mechanical characterization is the next step toward clinical application.

title: Long-Term Volumetric Outcomes and Response Patterns Following Gamma Knife Radiosurgery for Large Vestibular Schwannomas: Impact of Tumor Composition.
abstract: Objective The optimal management of large vestibular schwannoma (VS) remains controversial. While microsurgical resection has traditionally been preferred due to tumor size and mass effect, it is associated with considerable morbidity. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Gamma Knife radiosurgery (GKRS) for large VS, with a particular focus on long-term volumetric changes and factors influencing tumor shrinkage. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 36 patients with large VS (volume >5 cc) who underwent GKRS between April 2005 and January 2023. Tumor volume was assessed using three-dimensional volumetric analysis. The residual tumor volume ratio was calculated as the percentage of the post-treatment volume relative to baseline. Factors associated with tumor volume reduction were analyzed using linear and logistic regression models. Tumor response patterns, including pseudoprogression, were also evaluated longitudinally. Results The median baseline tumor volume was 7.3 cc, with a median follow-up duration of 69 months. Radiographic tumor control rate was 97%. The median residual tumor volume ratio was 26.1% (median 2.4 cc), indicating substantial tumor shrinkage after GKRS. In the continuous analysis, cystic composition was associated with a lower final residual tumor volume ratio than solid composition (adjusted geometric mean ratio, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.26-0.78; p=0.006). In multivariable logistic regression, the dependent variable was a final residual tumor volume ratio ≥25% of baseline. Cystic VS was associated with lower odds of this outcome than solid VS (OR, 0.056; 95% CI, 0.004-0.385, p=0.002). Furthermore, cystic tumors were significantly more likely to exhibit continuous shrinkage pattern, whereas solid tumors were more prone to pseudoprogression. Additionally, pseudoprogression persisted for up to 5 years before subsequent regression, with transient volume expansion reaching as high as 3.6 times the initial tumor volume. During follow-up, complications occurred in 4 patients (11%); two required shunt placement. One additional patient (2.8%) underwent salvage microsurgery for intractable trigeminal neuralgia despite radiographic tumor shrinkage. Conclusion In this selected retrospective cohort of patients with large VS, GKRS was associated with high observed radiographic tumor control and substantial tumor shrinkage. Cystic composition was associated with greater volume reduction in exploratory analyses. Because delayed regression can follow transient enlargement, careful imaging interpretation and long-term follow-up are important to distinguish pseudoprogression from true tumor progression. These findings require validation in larger comparative studies.

title: Unimodal imaging foundation models and vision-language models in MRI: A systematic review of emerging methods and clinical applications.
abstract: Artificial intelligence in medical imaging is shifting from task-specific algorithms toward adaptable foundation models (FMs) and vision-language models (VLMs). However, applying these models to MRI remains challenging because clinical interpretation requires integrating multi-parametric, volumetric imaging across multiple sequences with clinical context. This systematic review evaluates 35 studies on unimodal FMs and multimodal VLMs in MRI, summarizing emerging architectures, downstream applications, and challenges to clinical translation. Current research is concentrated in neuroimaging, with diagnostic classification representing the most mature application. Segmentation and outcome prediction also show promise, whereas automated report generation remains limited by poor clinical fidelity despite strong linguistic fluency. Broader adoption is hindered by heterogeneous MRI acquisition, limited large-scale paired image-text datasets, and inadequate safety-focused evaluation metrics. Advancing clinical translation will require standardized multicenter datasets, stronger integration with electronic health records and pathology, robust evaluation frameworks, and improved model explainability.

title: Spatial omics in cancer: a review of computational approaches and vision of AI-driven analysis.
abstract: Predicting patient response to cancer treatments remains a challenge due to tumor heterogeneity and complex tumor microenvironments (TMEs). Modern spatial genomics technologies enable gene expression profiling alongside histological frameworks, but comprehensive analysis and clinical translation of these high-dimensionality datasets will benefit from Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML). This review synthesizes computational approaches that address challenges of spatial data by examining deep-learning architectures such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for histological feature extraction and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for modeling cell-cell interactions. We then explore the paradigm of Foundation Models that bridge histopathology with transcriptomics to accelerate the identification of spatially resolved biomarkers, improve patient stratification for immunotherapy and targeted treatments, and advance the clinical translation of mechanistic insights derived from the tumor microenvironment.

title: Novel orthotopic uterine leiomyosarcoma model demonstrated enhanced tumor growth, metastasis, and chemosensitivity compared to subcutaneous counterparts.
abstract: Objective Uterine leiomyosarcoma (uLMS) maintains a poor prognosis due to its aggressive behavior and limited therapeutic response. Preclinical progress is severely hindered by traditional subcutaneous models that often fail to metastasize, despite one-third of uLMS patients displaying metastases at diagnosis. This study aimed to establish a reproducible, physiologically accurate orthotopic uLMS murine model that faithfully recapitulates disease progression and chemotherapeutic response. Methods Primary subcutaneous tumors were established via SK-LMS-1 cell injections in NOD/SCID mice. Harvested xenografts were surgically implanted heterotopically (subcutaneous flank) or orthotopically (uterine myometrium). Eight days post-implantation, mice were randomized to receive intraperitoneal doxorubicin (1.2 mg/kg twice weekly) or vehicle control for 3 weeks. Tumor growth was tracked longitudinally via MRI (orthotopic) or caliper measurement (subcutaneous). Immunohistochemistry evaluated tumor vitality, microenvironment hypoxia, vascular density, and metastatic spread. Results Orthotopic tumors exhibited significantly accelerated growth kinetics compared to subcutaneous counterparts. This expansion was supported by co-option of host uterine vasculature, resulting in ample tumor perfusion, suppressed tissue hypoxia, and robust proliferation. Crucially, 37% of primary orthotopic tumors developed spontaneous, multi-organ metastases to pulmonary, omental, and intraperitoneal sites by 4 weeks. Orthotopic tumors demonstrated heightened sensitivity to doxorubicin, achieving a 55% volume reduction compared to 44% in subcutaneous controls, mediated by superior intratumoral drug delivery supported by increased cleaved caspase-3-dependent apoptosis. Conclusions Surgical orthotopic xenografting recapitulates clinical uLMS, demonstrating site-dependent vascular co-option, spontaneous systemic metastasis, and enhanced chemosensitivity. By mimicking physiological characteristics of human uLMS, this orthotopic model offers significant potential for enhancing understanding of uLMS and evaluating novel therapies.

title: Superpixel-ComBat multi-site harmonization of unpaired T1W MRI data in Huntington's disease.
abstract: Background Pooling multi-site MRI data is essential for well-powered neuroimaging analyses, particularly in Huntington's disease (HD), where large cohorts are needed to study disease-stage heterogeneity and subtle progressive neuroanatomical change. However, scanner-related variability hinders direct data pooling, confounding image-level methods such as voxel-based morphometry (VBM). Superpixel-ComBat (SP-ComBat), a voxel-level image-harmonization framework, effectively removes scanner effects but depends on traveling-subject data that are rarely available retrospectively. To extend SP-ComBat to unpaired multi-site T1-weighted MRI by introducing a pseudo-pairing framework that leverages demographically matched controls across scanners as surrogate traveling subjects. Methods Two pipelines were developed to estimate scanner effects under retrospective constraints: pipeline 1 used a small set of well-matched pseudo-pairs (n = 4) with bootstrap resampling to address scanners with limited sample sizes, while pipeline 2 used the recommended number of pseudo-pairs (n = 16) without resampling. Pseudo-pair images were parcellated into 3D-superpixels, and ComBat was applied within clusters to estimate scanner-specific adjustments for native-space harmonization. Pipeline performance was assessed in a representative multi-study dataset comprising six scanners from three HD cohorts (HD-YAS, HD-CSF, TRACK-HD; N = 144) and replicated in the full multi-study dataset (FMD; N = 538). Results Both pipelines improved image quality, aligned scanner-specific intensities, and preserved disease-related structural patterns. Pipeline 2 showed superior parameter re-estimation stability and was selected for the FMD. Harmonization eliminated systematic segmentation errors, enabled a single unified VBM pipeline across scanners, and increased sensitivity to HD-related voxel-wise atrophy. Conclusions SP-ComBat was effectively adapted for harmonization of unpaired multi-site structural MRI, reducing scanner bias while preserving biological variability and supporting unified VBM analyses across scanners.

title: Surface-based cortical morphometry in fibromyalgia reveals left temporal lobe thinning and dissociated thickness-area patterns: a FreeSurfer replication and extension study.
abstract: Background Fibromyalgia (FM) is a nociplastic pain disorder associated with structural brain changes. Surface-based cortical thickness analysis using FreeSurfer, enabling independent measurement of cortical thickness and surface area, has been applied to FM in only a small number of studies. Methods We applied FreeSurfer 7.4.1 to structural MRI from 20 women with FM and 20 age-matched healthy controls from OpenNeuro dataset ds001928 (GE 3T SPGR), previously analysed by Agoalikum et al. using source-based morphometry (SBM). Group comparisons of 68 Desikan-Killiany cortical parcels and 16 subcortical structures used Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction, covarying for age (and eTIV for volumes). Results Three cortical regions survived FDR correction (q < 0.05), all left temporal: inferior temporal cortex (d = -1.77), fusiform gyrus (d = -1.35), and middle temporal gyrus (d = -1.22); a whole-surface vertex-wise GLM independently confirmed this left temporal thinning and additionally resolved entorhinal involvement. A thickness-area dissociation was identified: middle temporal gyrus showed laminar thinning (thickness reduced, area preserved), whereas inferior temporal cortex showed concurrent thickness and area reduction. Subcortical findings included bilateral cerebellar cortex reduction (d ∼ -1.0), right amygdala reduction (d = -1.01), and bilateral pallidum enlargement (d≈+0.85); all FDR q < 0.05. Thalamic volumes did not differ between groups (p > .54), directly contradicting the main finding of the prior SBM analysis on the same subjects. Left ACC cortical thickness correlated inversely with depression severity in this FM cohort (age-adjusted GLM: partial r = -0.65, p = .003, FDR q = 0.022). Conclusions SBM and surface-based morphometry capture distinct structural properties in FM even when applied to identical subjects, with implications for methodological standardisation. Temporal association cortex may represent a candidate structural substrate for the cognitive symptoms of FM, though this interpretation is provisional as no cognitive measures were available in this cohort.

title: Deep learning denoising and positron range correction of clinical [ 68 Ga]Ga-DOTA-TOC PET images.
abstract: PET image quality degradation due to positron range effects in high-energy positron-emitting radionuclides such as Gallium-68 ( 68 Ga) can be mitigated by applying positron range correction (PRC). Deep learning (DL) models have been shown to improve image quality by reducing image noise. This study aimed to evaluate a DL model for simultaneous denoising and 68 Ga-specific PRC in clinical [ 68 Ga]Ga-DOTA-TOC PET scans. Three different U-Net-based DL models were trained to map reduced-count PET images reconstructed without PRC (25%, 33%, or 50% of acquired counts) to full-count PET images reconstructed with tissue-independent PRC (FC-PRC). The generated reduced-count-enhanced images (RCE-25%, RCE-33%, RCE-50%) were evaluated using the mean standardized uptake value (SUV mean ) in liver and lung, noise levels in liver, and maximum standardized uptake value (SUV max ) and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of soft tissue lesions. Three experienced nuclear medicine physicians assessed the overall image quality (OIQ), overall diagnostic confidence (ODC), and lesion detectability (sensitivity, specificity, accuracy). Compared to FC-PRC, RCE-33% and RCE-50% exhibited similar noise, whereas RCE-25% showed substantial residual noise. CNR was reduced for RCE-33% (-5.6%, p=0.001) and RCE-25% (-8.0%, p<0.001), but was comparable for RCE-50%. All reduced-count-enhanced images demonstrated lower SUV max (RCE-25%: -3.8%, p=0.02; RCE-33%: -7.0%, p<0.001; RCE-50%: -5.2%, p<0.001). RCE-33% and RCE-50% achieved non-inferior OIQ and ODC compared to FC-PRC, while RCE-25% demonstrated only non-inferior ODC. All reduced-count-enhanced images showed high sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy (>90%). The proposed DL-based approach achieved comparable noise and image quality down to 50% of counts. Although it did not outperform the reconstruction-based PRC, its benefit lies in simultaneous denoising and PRC in a single step.

title: Multicenter evaluation of total body irradiation planning strategies: A DGMP working group study on large-field irradiation techniques.
abstract: Purpose Total body irradiation (TBI) is an integral component of conditioning regimens for hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Despite similar biological objectives, planning and delivery of TBI vary substantially across institutions. The aim of this study was to quantitatively assess inter-institutional and technique-dependent variability in contemporary TBI planning by comparing dose distributions generated under standardized conditions across multiple centers in Germany and Switzerland. Methods Twenty-four radiotherapy centers received anonymized total-body computed tomography (CT) datasets of a standardized dummy patient in head-first supine and prone orientations, including predefined points of interest (POI) and organs at risk (OARs). Each center was asked to generate TBI plans for two prescription levels (8 Gy in 4 fractions and 12 Gy in 6 fractions) using its local planning standards, with the entire body defined as the planning target volume (PTV). Submissions included treatment-planning-system (TPS)-based 3D dose distributions and in-house table-based calculations. TPS plans were centrally imported into a TPS for extraction of target coverage and OAR dose metrics, while table-based submissions were evaluated using aggregated POI doses. Results In total, 45 TBI treatment plans from 24 centers were analyzed, including 24 plans for 8 Gy and 21 plans for 12 Gy. Both TPS-based and table-based planning approaches were represented across a broad range of clinical techniques, including volumetic modulated arc therapy (VMAT), Tomotherapy, sweeping beam, static field, bilateral, and translation couch setups. Marked inter-institutional variability was observed, particularly for lung, lens, and kidney doses. At the 12 Gy prescription level, mean lung doses differed by more than 3 Gy between centers, corresponding to relative variations of up to approximately 30%. Conformal intensity-modulated techniques (VMAT and Tomotherapy) showed the highest consistency across institutions, whereas non-conformal approaches exhibited substantially larger dose variability. Increased lung sparing at 12 Gy was consistently associated with reduced target coverage compared to 8 Gy. Conclusion This study provides the first standardized multicenter planning-based comparison of contemporary TBI approaches in Germany and Switzerland. By quantifying inter-institutional variability in dose distributions under uniform conditions, the results outline the current heterogeneity of clinical practice and the range of achievable dosimetric outcomes. Rather than defining a reference standard, these findings establish a structured benchmark of existing planning strategies and highlight the need for harmonization, thereby providing a foundation for future consensus development and end-to-end validation efforts.

title: Impact of ROI definition on head and neck cancer FDG-PET radiomics.
abstract: Due to its rising incidence, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) represents a global health challenge, and risk stratification is important for personalized treatment. 18 F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)-derived biomarkers show considerable potential for predicting HNSCC radio(chemo)therapy outcomes. However, the definition of the three-dimensional primary tumor region of interest (ROI) varies, with anatomically defined gross tumor volumes (GTV-ROIs) and PET-based metabolic tumor volumes (MTV-ROIs) often used interchangeably. Therefore, we assessed the effect of these ROI definitions on extracted radiomics features and radio(chemo)therapy outcome predictions in a multicenter dataset of 741 HNSCC patients. Features from the two ROI definitions were compared using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). The investigated study endpoints, locoregional control (LRC) and overall survival (OS), were evaluated using the number of outcome-associated features in univariate Cox regression, as well as by the performance of multivariable machine-learning models. GTV-ROIs and MTV-ROIs yielded substantially different radiomics features, with a median ICC of 0.63 (IQR, 0.37-0.85). The MTV-ROIs led to a higher number of OS-associated features (continuous features: p = 0.003, binarized features: p = 0.015) and comparable model C-indexes, 0.61 (95% CI: 0.51-0.69; MTV-ROIs) vs.0.58 (95% CI: 0.49-0.66; GTV-ROIs) for LRC, and 0.65 (95% CI: 0.59-0.71; MTV-ROIs) vs.0.63 (95% CI: 0.56-0.69; GTV-ROIs) for OS. To conclude, the definition of the HNSCC primary tumor ROI has a notable effect on FDG-PET feature values and their prognostic potential, whereas its effect on multivariable model performance appears limited.

title: Activity and safety of first-line pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel in triple-negative breast cancer: a single-arm, phase 1b/2 trial.
abstract: Background Pumitamig, an investigational bispecific antibody targeting programmed death ligand-1 and vascular endothelial growth factor A, has shown preliminary efficacy across several tumour types. We aimed to evaluate the safety and activity of pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel as first-line treatment in patients with advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer. Methods In this single-arm, phase 1b/2 trial conducted at ten sites (hospitals and cancer centres) in China, patients aged 18-75 years with histologically documented, unresectable, locally advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer, an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 1 or less, and one or more measurable lesion (as per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours, version 1.1) received first-line pumitamig (20 mg/kg intravenously once every 2 weeks) plus nab-paclitaxel (100 mg/m 2 intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of each 28-day cycle) until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. In phase 1b, six patients received pumitamig (20 mg/kg once every 2 weeks intravenously plus nab-paclitaxel 100 mg/m 2 intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of each 28-day cycle) and were monitored for treatment-emergent adverse events, before subsequent enrolment in phase 2. The primary endpoints were confirmed objective response rate and safety, assessed in the efficacy-evaluable population, defined as all patients who received one or more doses of study drug and had measurable disease at baseline and at least one efficacy assessment. This trial is registered with chictr.org.cn (ChiCTR2200060400) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05918133), and is closed to recruitment. Findings Between June 27, 2022, and March 15, 2023, 42 patients were enrolled, received one or more doses of pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel (median duration of exposure 9·0 months, 95% CI 6·9-11·7) and had one or more tumour assessments. All patients were Chinese and female; median age was 53 years (IQR 41-60). At a median follow-up of 35·2 months (95% CI 33·0-36·1), the confirmed objective response rate was 73·8% (95% CI 58·0-86·1; 31 of 42 patients), including one complete response and 30 partial responses. The most frequent treatment-related adverse events of grade 3 or worse were decreased neutrophil count (13 [31%] of 42 patients), decreased white blood cell count (11 [26%]), proteinuria (six [14%]), and febrile neutropenia (five [12%]). Nine (21%) patients reported 14 treatment-related serious adverse events (alanine aminotransferase increased n=2; febrile neutropenia n=2; pancreatitis n=2; and ascites, aspartate aminotransferase increased, abdominal distension, γ-glutamyltransferase increased, blood alkaline phosphatase increased, cataract, macular oedema, and retinal vein occlusion all n=1). Treatment-related adverse events led to discontinuation of both nab-paclitaxel and pumitamig in four (10%) patients, discontinuation of nab-paclitaxel only in three (7%) patients, and discontinuation of pumitamig only in two (5%) patients. There were no treatment-related deaths. Interpretation Treatment with first-line pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel showed encouraging antitumour activity in patients with advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer and a safety profile consistent with the mode of actions of both agents. These findings warrant further clinical evaluation in global phase 2 and 3 trials. Funding Biotheus (BioNTech group). Background

Pumitamig, an investigational bispecific antibody targeting programmed death ligand-1 and vascular endothelial growth factor A, has shown preliminary efficacy across several tumour types. We aimed to evaluate the safety and activity of pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel as first-line treatment in patients with advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer.

Methods

In this single-arm, phase 1b/2 trial conducted at ten sites (hospitals and cancer centres) in China, patients aged 18-75 years with histologically documented, unresectable, locally advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer, an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 1 or less, and one or more measurable lesion (as per Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours, version 1.1) received first-line pumitamig (20 mg/kg intravenously once every 2 weeks) plus nab-paclitaxel (100 mg/m2 intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of each 28-day cycle) until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. In phase 1b, six patients received pumitamig (20 mg/kg once every 2 weeks intravenously plus nab-paclitaxel 100 mg/m2 intravenously on days 1, 8, and 15 of each 28-day cycle) and were monitored for treatment-emergent adverse events, before subsequent enrolment in phase 2. The primary endpoints were confirmed objective response rate and safety, assessed in the efficacy-evaluable population, defined as all patients who received one or more doses of study drug and had measurable disease at baseline and at least one efficacy assessment. This trial is registered with chictr.org.cn (ChiCTR2200060400) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05918133), and is closed to recruitment.

Findings

Between June 27, 2022, and March 15, 2023, 42 patients were enrolled, received one or more doses of pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel (median duration of exposure 9·0 months, 95% CI 6·9-11·7) and had one or more tumour assessments. All patients were Chinese and female; median age was 53 years (IQR 41-60). At a median follow-up of 35·2 months (95% CI 33·0-36·1), the confirmed objective response rate was 73·8% (95% CI 58·0-86·1; 31 of 42 patients), including one complete response and 30 partial responses. The most frequent treatment-related adverse events of grade 3 or worse were decreased neutrophil count (13 [31%] of 42 patients), decreased white blood cell count (11 [26%]), proteinuria (six [14%]), and febrile neutropenia (five [12%]). Nine (21%) patients reported 14 treatment-related serious adverse events (alanine aminotransferase increased n=2; febrile neutropenia n=2; pancreatitis n=2; and ascites, aspartate aminotransferase increased, abdominal distension, γ-glutamyltransferase increased, blood alkaline phosphatase increased, cataract, macular oedema, and retinal vein occlusion all n=1). Treatment-related adverse events led to discontinuation of both nab-paclitaxel and pumitamig in four (10%) patients, discontinuation of nab-paclitaxel only in three (7%) patients, and discontinuation of pumitamig only in two (5%) patients. There were no treatment-related deaths.

Interpretation

Treatment with first-line pumitamig plus nab-paclitaxel showed encouraging antitumour activity in patients with advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer and a safety profile consistent with the mode of actions of both agents. These findings warrant further clinical evaluation in global phase 2 and 3 trials.

Funding

Biotheus (BioNTech group).

title: Cancer in the Commonwealth: a Lancet Oncology Commission.
abstract: Cancer is now one of the defining health and development challenges of our time. The 56 nations of the Commonwealth, home to 2·7 billion people, mirror this global burden. Recorded cancer cases across member states rose by 35% in 2008-18 and the number of deaths reached almost 1·7 million in 2018. The Lancet Oncology Commission on cancer in the Commonwealth was convened to ask a deceptively simple question: how can 56 diverse nations act collectively to close the widening gap between the burden of cancer and the capacity of each country to respond? 80 researchers, clinicians, policy makers, and civil society members, organised into five working groups and ten research streams, spent 2 years assembling the evidence base for this report. Using a validated microsimulation model, we estimate that 5-year net survival across eleven common cancers in the Commonwealth stood at just 30·7% in 2020, ranging from 4·1% in low-income countries (LICs) to 59·0% in high-income countries (HICs), driven overwhelmingly by late-stage presentation, which affects 62% of patients in LICs compared with 43% in HICs. This difference in survival is compounded by chronic underinvestment. Infrastructure gaps are equally stark: only 12% of countries meet international benchmarks for CT imaging, 22% for hospital density, and 40% for radiotherapy. Governance is underdeveloped too: barely one-third of Commonwealth countries have a national cancer control plan meeting basic quality criteria. Research investment also mirrors these inequities: between 2016 and 2023, Commonwealth countries collectively invested only US$165 per cancer-related disability adjusted life year. Yet the case for investment is unambiguous. Our modelling shows that a comprehensive scaleup of treatment, imaging, and quality of care could raise 5-year net survival across the Commonwealth from 30·7% to 52·9%, averting an estimated 5·8 million deaths and adding 113 million life-years between 2025 and 2035, at an incremental cost of $36·7 billion, delivering a return of between four and twenty dollars on every dollar invested. Crucially, this investment need not depend chiefly on external aid, which is contracting sharply at present. Our modelling for 38 low-income and middle-income Commonwealth countries suggests that up to $701 billion in additional domestic fiscal space could be mobilised between 2025 and 2030, through budget reprioritisation, macroeconomic growth, targeted taxation, and prudent borrowing. On this evidence, the Commission proposes six priority actions. These commitments are ambitious, set against an unusually turbulent geopolitical backdrop of declining official development assistance, fiscal retrenchment, and contested multilateralism. Yet it is precisely this backdrop that gives the Commonwealth its distinctive advantage: a voluntary association spanning every income level and continent, bound by common legal and regulatory traditions, capable of collective action that neither purely bilateral aid nor multilateral institutions under strain can easily replicate.

title: Contralateral tonsillectomy in oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma: diagnostic yield and procedural burden.
abstract: Objective Unilateral radiotherapy for well-lateralised oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma reduces treatment toxicity. This study evaluated whether routine contralateral tonsillectomy, performed to look for synchronous tonsillar malignancies, is justified. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted of 81 patients treated with curative intent for oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma at a tertiary centre (2022-2024). All patients underwent positron emission tomography computed tomography. Contralateral tonsillectomy was performed in candidates for unilateral radiotherapy. Results Forty-two patients underwent contralateral tonsillectomy. Synchronous contralateral squamous cell carcinoma was identified in one patient (2.4 per cent) who required bilateral cervical chemoradiation because of extranodal extension found on neck dissection. Eleven patients (26 per cent) underwent staged procedures after a median interval of 21 days. Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage requiring hospital re-admission occurred in one patient (2.4 per cent). Conclusion Routine contralateral tonsillectomy did not yield any findings that altered the laterality of treatment in any patient. This suggests that omitting contralateral tonsillectomy may complement de-escalation strategies.

title: Pericarditis in COVID-19: a focus on the paediatric population.
abstract: Background COVID-19, caused by SARS-CoV-2, is primarily a respiratory illness but may cause cardiovascular complications, including pericarditis. Pediatric SARS-CoV-2-associated pericarditis remains uncommon and likely underreported. This review summarizes the epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, management, and outcomes of pericarditis associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection in children. Methods We narratively reviewed the available literature on SARS-CoV-2-associated pericarditis in the pediatric population, including isolated acute pericarditis, myopericarditis, pericardial effusion, cardiac tamponade, and pericardial involvement in multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C). Results The true incidence of pediatric SARS-CoV-2-associated pericarditis remains unclear. Reported cases suggest that older children and adolescents are more commonly affected, typically presenting with chest pain, fever, dyspnea, or tachycardia, whereas younger children may exhibit nonspecific symptoms. Diagnosis relies on clinical criteria supported by electrocardiography, echocardiography, inflammatory markers, and cardiac biomarkers, with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging useful when myocardial involvement is suspected. Available evidence suggests a predominantly immune-mediated pathophysiology involving cytokine dysregulation and systemic inflammation, with limited evidence of direct viral invasion. Management is largely extrapolated from established pediatric pericarditis principles and adult data. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and colchicine are first-line therapies, while corticosteroids or intravenous immunoglobulin may be considered in selected inflammatory or MIS-C-associated cases, and interleukin-1 blockade in refractory or recurrent disease. Most affected children recover, although severe pericardial effusion, tamponade, and recurrence have been reported. Conclusion Pediatric SARS-CoV-2-associated pericarditis encompasses a spectrum of clinical presentations and generally carries a favorable prognosis. Nevertheless, potentially serious complications emphasize the importance of early recognition, differentiation from myocarditis and MIS-C, and structured follow-up.

title: Band-Pass Fluorescence Activation via Dual-Responsive Molecular Design in the NIR-II Window for In Vivo pH Sensing.
abstract: Real-time monitoring of physiological pH in living systems is essential for accurate disease evaluation and therapeutic guidance. However, conventional pH-responsive probes typically operate through monotonic activation and lack window selectivity, limiting their capacity to report further microenvironmental changes after crossing the activation threshold. Here, we report a NIR-II molecularly engineered band-pass pH (BPpH) sensing strategy that exhibits a non-monotonic "off-on-off" fluorescence response. By integrating an acid-responsive spirolactam switch with an alkaline-sensitive phenolic regulator, the BPpH probes enable window-restricted signal output within a defined pH range. BPpH-3 displays fluorescence activation from pH 3.6 to 5.2 and deactivation from pH 5.2 to 8.0, affording dual apparent pKa values of 4.16 and 7.42 and establishing a response window. Unlike conventional monotonic turn-on probes, this band-pass response enables continuous tracking of pH changes across the therapeutic process, and BPpH-3 further enables dynamic evaluation of therapeutic efficacy in a skin inflammation model, allowing timely assessment of treatment progression and dosing sufficiency. Moreover, its window-constrained response mitigates signal over-amplification under extreme acidification, facilitating improved tumor margin delineation for precision resection under NIR-II imaging guidance. The band-pass sensing strategy presented here provides a transferable framework for window-regulated detection of diverse physiological parameters and holds promise for integration with multiple diagnostic imaging modalities.

title: An Enzyme-Triggered Self-Immobilizing Dual-Modal Probe for Precision Imaging and Sustained Gas Therapy of Early-Stage MASH.
abstract: The clinical management of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is hindered by the lack of noninvasive molecular diagnostics and effective targeted therapies. Although hydrogen sulfide (H2S) can ameliorate MASH via antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, conventional H2S donors suffer from uncontrolled burst release and rapid in vivo clearance. Here, we report AzoR-Cy-Gd, a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)/fluorescence imaging (FLI)-guided H2S theranostic platform for early diagnosis, severity assessment, and visualized intervention of MASH. This hypoxia-responsive theranostic probe, featuring a reductively cleavable azo linkage, integrates a near-infrared cyanine fluorophore, a Gd-DO3A MRI contrast unit, and a carbonyl sulfide (COS)/H2S-releasing module. In MASH lesions, hypoxia-associated reductive activation induces cleavage of the azo bond, which subsequently triggers a self-immolative cascade, generating quinone methide (QM) for in situ protein anchoring and releasing COS for carbonic anhydrase-mediated H2S production. This synchronized activation restores intramolecular charge transfer, producing a 50-fold fluorescence enhancement and increasing relaxivity (r1) from 8.9 to 14.1 mM-1 s-1 while prolonging lesion retention. In a methionine/choline-deficient diet-induced mouse model, AzoR-Cy-Gd sensitively visualized hepatic pathogenesis and tracked disease progression from 4 to 8 weeks. Moreover, localized H2S release effectively suppressed inflammation, reduced lipid accumulation, and restored liver architecture and function. Overall, AzoR-Cy-Gd establishes a self-reporting "see-and-treat" strategy for precision MASH theranostics.

title: Acid-Catalyzed Synthesis of Octacosanyl Fatty Acid Esters and Their In Vivo Biological Activities.
abstract: Octacosanol (C28), mainly found in rice bran and sugar cane, possesses cholesterol-lowering properties but is limited by poor bioavailability. This study optimized the sulfuric acid-catalyzed synthesis of lauric acid-esterified octacosanol (LEO) and oleic acid-esterified octacosanol (OEO) to enhance their bioactivity. Under optimized conditions (140-150 °C for 3 h), esterification rates reached 97.8% for LEO and 90.6% for OEO, with structures confirmed via gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS), nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and Fourier transform infrared spectrometer (FTIR). In high-fat diet-induced obese C57BL/6J mice, both esters significantly improved serum lipid profiles compared to nonesterified octacosanol, with OEO showing the strongest efficacy in reducing total cholesterol and elevating HDL-c. Furthermore, a 28-day subacute toxicological assessment in ICR mice revealed no clinical, biochemical, or hematological abnormalities, indicating a favorable preliminary safety profile for OEO. These results suggest that OEO is a promising functional ingredient for mitigating hyperlipidemia and cardiovascular disease risk, offering improved application potential in dietary supplements.

title: Evaluation and an Exploratory Human Study of 99mTc-Labeled PSMA-Targeting Agents with Reduced Renal Uptake via Proline Incorporation.
abstract: Excessive renal uptake of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceuticals remains a major challenge in prostate cancer (PCa) detection and therapy. We developed 99mTc-labeled PSMA radioligands incorporating d- or l-proline as a conformationally constrained linker combined with optimized co-ligands to reduce kidney accumulation. The resulting hydrophilic complexes achieved high radiochemical yields and strong in vitro stability. The optimal radiotracer, [99mTc]Tc-L-M1, exhibited high LNCaP (PSMA++) cell affinity (Kd = 19.09 nM) and the lowest kidney uptake (6.50 ± 0.32% ID/g, Kunming mice, 2 h p.i.). It accumulated effectively in both LNCaP (PSMA++) and 22Rv1 (PSMA+) tumors with excellent target-to-nontarget ratios and strong PSMA specificity. SPECT/CT imaging confirmed low renal accumulation, consistent with biodistribution data. Preliminary clinical trials demonstrated clear delineation of small PCa lesions, highlighting [99mTc]Tc-L-M1 as a promising PSMA-specific radiotracer with reduced kidney uptake for clinical application.

title: Development and Preclinical Evaluation of [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-L3: A Novel PET Tracer for Quantitative Imaging of Carbonic Anhydrase IX.
abstract: Carbonic anhydrase IX (CA IX) is a key biomarker for tumor hypoxia and a promising target for molecular imaging. In this study, we developed [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-L3, a novel small-molecule CA IX-targeted PET tracer. The radiolabeling was optimized to consistently achieve a radiochemical purity of >98% (10 μg precursor, 90 °C, pH 4.5, 10 min), with excellent stability in saline and FBS up to 240 min. In vivo studies demonstrated rapid blood clearance and predominant renal excretion. Surface plasmon resonance analysis demonstrated high-affinity binding of the DOTA-L3 precursor toward CA IX (Kd = 7.60 ± 0.37 nM) with highest affinity observed for CA IX among the tested isoforms. MicroPET/CT imaging (30-240 min p.i.) showed robust tumor accumulation in OSRC-2 (SUVmean = 1.47 ± 0.21) and HT-29 (SUVmean = 1.03 ± 0.12) xenografts, while minimal uptake was observed in CA IX-low FTC-238 tumors (SUVmean = 0.21 ± 0.05) at 60 min p.i. PET-derived tumor uptake showed a strong linear correlation with CA IX expression levels (R2 = 0.976, P < 0.001) across the three tumor models. High tumor-to-muscle and tumor-to-blood ratios further confirm favorable imaging contrast (T/M = 27.53 ± 1.89 and T/B = 24.61 ± 2.35 at 240 min p.i. for OSRC-2 model). These results support [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-L3 as a promising candidate for non-invasive assessment of CA IX-associated hypoxia and as a scaffold for future theranostic development.

title: Design and Application of Platinum-Functionalized Iron Oxide Nanoparticles in a Radiosensitization Context.
abstract: Cancer remains a major public health burden, and radiotherapy is widely used as a central therapeutic modality. Improving the therapeutic window of radiotherapy remains a major challenge, particularly through strategies able to optimize the destruction of tumor cells while minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissues. Iron oxide nanoparticles (IONPs) are promising biomedical platforms due to their imaging capabilities, including magnetic resonance imaging and magnetic particle imaging. Nevertheless, their intrinsic radiosensitizing effect remains moderate compared to other nanoparticle-based or molecular radiosensitizers. Here, an IONP-based nanoplatform functionalized with platinum complexes was developed to enhance radiosensitization in lung cancer cells. The synthesis and physicochemical characterization of platinum-functionalized IONPs are reported, as well as their chemical stability in artificial plasma fluid. Their biological impact was evaluated on A549 lung cancer cells and compared to that of nonfunctionalized IONPs under irradiation conditions. Platinum functionalization led to stable hybrid nanomaterials exhibiting a significantly increased radiosensitizing effect compared to nonfunctionalized IONPs. Mechanistic investigations further suggest that this increased effect involves nuclear DNA damage and mitochondrial membrane potential disruption. These results confirm the relevance of platinum-functionalized IONPs as multifunctional nanoplatforms for radiosensitization in lung cancer models.

title: Long-Term Biodistribution and Safety Profile of Laser-Generated Gold Nanoparticles Following High-Dose Administration in Mice.
abstract: Gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) have emerged as versatile agents for a wide range of biomedical applications, including imaging, diagnostics, and therapy. While their use in modalities such as CT imaging and radiotherapy is particularly promising, these applications require high systemic doses (≥500 mg Au/kg), necessitating thorough evaluation of long-term biodistribution and safety profiles. Here, we present a comprehensive one-year assessment of Polyethylene glycol (PEG) -coated laser-synthesized AuNPs (mean core diameter ∼8 nm). After intravenous administration at a high dose, biodistribution was evaluated in healthy mice ( n = 8; 874 ± 56 mg Au/kg) using a serial CT imaging, with terminal ICP-AES validation, blood biochemistry, and histology performed in 5 of these animals. AuNPs exhibited prolonged blood circulation (half-life 21 ± 3 h) and accumulated predominantly in reticuloendothelial organs: 42.2 ± 3.6%ID/cm 3 in the liver and 40.2 ± 3.3%ID/cm 3 in the spleen, with one-year retention of 77.5% and 83.1%, respectively. Despite substantial hepatic and splenic retention, no histopathological changes were detected in any major organs, including kidney and liver. Serum biochemical markers of liver, kidney, and pancreatic function revealed no statistically significant differences between the treated and control groups. Only a slight elevation in aspartate aminotransferase (AST) was observed in two treated animals (184.1 and 187.8 U/L vs 118.3 ± 18.4 U/L in the control group), while all other liver function markers (ALT, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) remained unaltered. Additionally, tumor uptake was evaluated in two separate cohorts of mice bearing subcutaneous tumor models, mammary adenocarcinoma Ca755 ( n = 3, 809 ± 28 mg Au/kg) and melanoma B16F10 ( n = 3, 814 ± 45 mg Au/kg). AuNPs accumulated in tumor tissue, reaching 9.4 ± 1.9%ID/cm 3 for Ca755 and 5.3 ± 1.1%ID/cm 3 for B16F10. Overall, these results provide insight into the safety profile and tumor uptake of laser-synthesized AuNPs, supporting their potential as a platform for novel radiosensitizers and contrast agents.

title: Vitamin D deficiency, quantitative ultrasound parameters and bone biomarkers in adolescents.
abstract: Background Vitamin D is crucial for bone mineralization and skeletal growth during adolescence; nevertheless, deficiency remains widespread even in sun-rich regions. This study examined serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D [25(OH)D] levels and their associations with bone status and turnover markers in Mexican adolescents. Methods A cross-sectional analysis was performed on 914 participants aged 11-18 years residing in Tlaxcala, Mexico. Anthropometric, socioeconomic, and biochemical data were collected, including 25(OH)D, parathyroid hormone (PTH), fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), osteocalcin (OC), osteopontin (OPN), osteoprotegerin (OPG), and RANKL. Bone status was assessed using quantitative ultrasound (QUS) at the radius and tibia. Results The median 25(OH)D concentration was 19.8 ng/mL; 44.3% of adolescents were categorized as having insufficiency, and 50.4% as having deficiency. Girls showed significantly lower levels than boys (18.5 vs. 22.1 ng/mL, p < 0.0001) and a higher prevalence of deficiency (62% vs. 36%). Low bone mineral density (LBDM; Score Z ≤ -1) occurred in 18.7% at the radius and 24.3% at the tibia. Serum 25(OH)D was positively associated with OC (β = 0.28, p = 0.013) and OPN (β = 0.28, p = 0.034) and inversely with OPG (β = -1.86, p = 0.050), particularly among girls, while no associations were found with PTH, FGF23, RANKL, or QUS parameters. Conclusion These findings reveal widespread vitamin D deficiency and sex-specific alterations in bone remodeling, highlighting the need for early prevention strategies tailored to vulnerable adolescents. Impact Vitamin D deficiency is highly prevalent among adolescents in central Mexico, especially girls, despite abundant sunlight. In a large pediatric cohort, this study links serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D with bone turnover biomarkers and quantitative ultrasound measures, showing sex-specific associations with markers of bone formation and remodeling. These findings suggest that inadequate vitamin D may alter bone metabolism before detectable reductions in bone density occur, supporting early screening and targeted interventions for youth living under similar environmental and socioeconomic conditions.

title: Comparing MRI-based scoring systems for neuroprognostication in neonatal encephalopathy.
abstract: Background Neonatal encephalopathy (NE) remains a significant cause of neurodevelopmental impairment. However, which MRI-based scoring system best predicts 36-month outcomes remains unclear. Methods A prospective cohort of 102 neonates ≥36 weeks gestation with NE underwent early postnatal brain MRI. Images were scored using five established systems: Barkovich, Weeke, Trivedi, Rutherford, and NICHD-NRN. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were evaluated at 36 months. Prognostic performance was analyzed using logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic curves. The best predictive model was determined using pairwise correlation to reduce highly correlated variables, and then backward selection to optimize the linear regression model. Results The Weeke total score showed the highest predictive accuracy for Bayley Scales of Infant Development motor outcomes (AUC 0.7647). The Weeke gray matter subscore was most predictive of Child Behavior Checklist internalizing problems (AUC 0.7735). No scoring system reliably predicted cognitive, language, or externalizing problems (AUC < 0.7). The optimal motor outcomes prediction model included 5 Weeke variables: basal ganglia, posterior limb of internal capsule, perirolandic cortex, cerebellar hemorrhage location, and basal ganglia lactate. Conclusions MRI-based scoring systems have limited prognostic value beyond motor outcomes after NE. The Weeke score offers the most reliable motor prediction, achievable using only five parameters. Impact Existing MRI scoring systems have limited prognostic value beyond motor outcomes after neonatal encephalopathy. The Weeke score offers the most reliable motor prediction. Only 5 Weeke scoring system variables are needed to optimize motor prediction. Deep gray matter injury is associated with internalizing behavioral outcomes. A simplified, user-friendly prognostic model can support accurate outcome prediction by a broader range of clinicians.

title: MRI measures of oxygen extraction fraction in the subacute phase of mild neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.
abstract: Background Early identification of newborns with mild encephalopathy at risk of clinical progression is critical. Our group has previously demonstrated regional quantification of oxygen extraction fraction (OEF), a noninvasive MRI-derived measure of cerebral oxygen utilization in newborns with encephalopathy receiving therapeutic hypothermia (TH). This study evaluates whether regional OEF measured between 2 and 7 days of life distinguishes newborns with mild encephalopathy who are not treated with TH and subsequently exhibit clinical progression within the first day of life from those who remain clinically stable. Methods Vessel-specific OEF maps of the brain were obtained using the accelerated T 2 -relaxation-under-phase-contrast (aTRUPC) MRI technique from full-term newborns with mild encephalopathy and healthy controls. OEF was quantified across six predefined venous drainage regions. Results Fifty-three full-term newborns (28 with mild encephalopathy, 25 healthy controls) were enrolled. Seven newborns with mild encephalopathy showed clinical progression on the first day of life and received TH (TH group); the remaining did not receive TH (non-TH group). OEF was significantly lower in cortical regions in the TH group compared with healthy controls and the non-TH group. Conclusion Cortical OEF represents an innovative imaging biomarker. Prospective studies are needed to determine its value for risk stratification during the therapeutic window. Impact Early identification of newborns with mild encephalopathy at risk of progression remains challenging during the therapeutic window. Cortical oxygen extraction fraction (OEF) measured between 2 and 7 days of life was significantly lower in newborns who progressed within the first day of life than in newborns with mild encephalopathy who did not progress and healthy controls. Regional OEF may provide a noninvasive biomarker for early risk stratification and treatment decision-making in newborns with mild encephalopathy.

title: Magnetic resonance imaging of congenital brain malformations.
abstract: Congenital brain malformations can contribute to significant morbidity and mortality. Severity and prognosis depend on the character, extent, and anatomical localization as well as associated genetic syndromes and other organ system involvement. Correct diagnosis is crucial for early interventions including supportive therapies, prognostic and genetic counseling, medical management, and/or surgical correction. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) improves early diagnosis and prognostication. This review outlines clinical signs and symptoms that may warrant an MRI followed by an overview of various cerebral, posterior fossa, and vascular malformations, as well as corpus callosum abnormalities with representative MR images as well as recommendations on how to set up and optimally perform MRI. Lastly, this review presents perspectives and focus areas for further research. IMPACT: What is the key message of your article? Magnetic resonance imaging is a key component to the diagnosis and prognosis of congenital brain malformations. What does it add to the existing literature? This review provides an updated review on the current literature on congenital brain malformations as well as recommendations for integrating MRI into clinical practice. What is the impact? This review contributes with recommendations on what to expect when interpreting MR images of neonates with suspected congenital brain malformations.

title: Anatomy of periprostatic nerves and nerve-sparing strategy for radical prostatectomy.
abstract: Background Radical prostatectomy is an important curative treatment for localized prostate cancer, but postoperative urinary incontinence and erectile dysfunction substantially impair quality of life. Understanding individual variation in periprostatic nerves, fascia, and supporting structures is essential for balancing oncological control with functional preservation. This narrative review examines periprostatic nerve and fascial anatomy, nerve-sparing grading systems, established surgical techniques, and emerging adjuncts for individualized surgical planning. Methods PubMed was searched through July 2026 using 'prostate', 'pelvic autonomic nerve', 'neurovascular bundle', 'nerve sparing', 'radical prostatectomy', 'continence', 'erectile function', and 'NeuroSAFE'. Relevant guidelines and standard anatomical texts were also reviewed, alongside anatomical and clinical studies directly addressing periprostatic nerve anatomy, nerve-sparing techniques, or functional and oncological outcomes. Results Anatomical and histological studies show substantial variation in periprostatic nerve distribution. Nerve fibres are not confined to conventional posterolateral neurovascular bundles. Some extend into the anterolateral prostate and course through multilayered, heterogeneous fascial structures. Anatomy-based grading systems provide practical intraoperative frameworks but cannot accurately quantify nerve preservation in individual patients. Bilateral or more extensive nerve sparing is associated with better recovery of urinary continence and erectile function. However, these associations are influenced by baseline function, tumour risk, surgeon experience, and inconsistent outcome definitions. Contemporary approaches increasingly preserve a broader complex of nerves, fascia, and supporting structures. Refined techniques may improve early functional recovery, although comparative long-term evidence remains limited. Multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging, NeuroSAFE, and intraoperative nerve-identification technologies may further support individualized planning and real-time adjustment of dissection planes. Conclusions A detailed understanding of individualized periprostatic nerve and fascial anatomy underpins effective nerve-sparing surgery. Integrating anatomy-based grading, patient-specific planning, and advanced adjunctive technologies may improve the balance between oncological control and functional preservation.
