title: Expansion of the Inpatient Metastatic Spine Score to Outpatients With Spine Metastases: Prospective Assessment on an Ongoing Phase 2 Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: Objectives For inpatients with spinal metastases, the Inpatient Metastatic Spine Score accurately assesses prognosis, with scores of 0 to 3 exhibiting significantly longer survival than scores >3. This study examines the accuracy of this algorithm for outpatients prospectively considered for enrollment in the Spine Patient Optimal Radiosurgery Treatment for Symptomatic MEtastatic Neoplasms (SPORTSMEN) phase II randomized controlled trial. Methods From July 2025 to January 2026, outpatients at an NCI-designated cancer center were evaluated. Prognosis was assessed per an adjusted Metastatic Spine Score adjusted for consisting of: age at presentation (60+ vs. younger), duration of metastatic disease diagnosis (6+ mo vs. sooner), refractory to or on active systemic therapy (yes/no), additional nonspine metastatic focus (yes/no), severe malnutrition of chronic disease (yes/no), brain metastases (yes/no), and presenting symptomatology (asymptomatic or spine/back pain alone=no; additional neurological symptoms=yes) with each category scored a 0 (no) or 1 (yes) and a cumulative score derived. Scores of 0 to 3 were compared with scores >3 and correlated with outcomes. Positive prognosis=time to death/hospice >90 days from presentation. The Fisher test was used for statistical analysis. Results A positive prognosis was exhibited in 8/9 patients with scores of 0 to 3 (8/8 patients without brain metastases) versus 3/9 patients with scores >3 (P=0.0498). The overall accuracy of the Metastatic Spine Score (8/9 positive + 6/9 negative=14/18 patients) was 78%. Conclusion The Metastatic Spine Score provides an accurate prognostic assessment of outpatients with spine metastases, with scores of 0 to 3 yielding significantly better prognosis than scores >3. These findings also support brain MRI evaluation before radiotherapy decisions regarding spinal metastases. This study adds further support for establishing the Metastatic Spine Score as the standard-of-care for accurately evaluating prognosis in this patient population for outpatients as well as inpatients.

Conclusion

The Metastatic Spine Score provides an accurate prognostic assessment of outpatients with spine metastases, with scores of 0 to 3 yielding significantly better prognosis than scores >3. title: Racial, Ethnic, and Regional Influences on National Patterns of Mammographic Screening.
abstract: Objectives We sought to evaluate whether there were clinically significant disparities in screening mammography rates according to race, ethnicity, and United States geographic region in patients with access to health care systems. Methods We queried the Cosmos Epic national database to ascertain mammographic screening rates for women aged 50 to 65 who had 1 or more ambulatory encounters with a primary care physician between November 9, 2020, and November 8, 2023. Patients with a previous breast cancer and those with missing race or ethnicity data were excluded. Results The overall mammographic screening rate was 63.8% in the 7,837,164 individuals who met study criteria. There were no clinically meaningful differences in screening according to race. However, screening was less frequent in those with Hispanic ethnicity versus non-Hispanic (58.9% vs. 64.3%, P<0.001). Rates also varied according to region, with the lowest rates in the West (55.5%, P<0.001). Screening rates for Black and White groups were within 5% of one another in all 4 regions. With respect to ethnicity, the South was the only region where the Hispanic population rate had a lower rate over 5% (61.8% vs. 55.7%, P<0.001). Conclusions Many patients receiving health care in the US do not receive recommended mammogram screening, but there were no clinically significant differences by race. Lower rates were noted in Hispanic populations, particularly in the South. Targeted educational and community outreach efforts in this region are warranted.

title: What Are the Oncologic Outcomes of Patients With Osteosarcoma and Venous Tumor Thrombi Managed by an Aggressive Multidisciplinary Approach of Chemotherapy and Surgical Resection?
abstract: Background Macroscopic venous tumor thrombus (VTT) is a rare but aggressive manifestation of osteosarcoma that poses substantial challenges for both surgical management and systemic disease control. Our previous work characterized its frequency, radiographic features, and adverse prognostic association, particularly in pelvic osteosarcoma; however, surgical management was heterogeneous. The patient-level outcomes achieved after a standardized multidisciplinary treatment approach and the association between VTT resection strategy and postoperative oncologic outcomes remain unclear. Questions/purposes (1) What were the oncologic outcomes of patients with osteosarcoma with macroscopic VTT treated under a standardized treatment algorithm incorporating aggressive surgical resection? (2) Did the choice of VTT resection strategy affect oncologic outcomes? Methods We screened the records of 39 patients with treatment-naive osteosarcoma and macroscopic VTT identified on imaging who were treated according to a standardized multimodal treatment algorithm between 2019 and 2024. This algorithm consisted of standardized multimodal imaging at diagnosis to detect and characterize VTT. After biopsy confirmation, patients received four-agent neoadjuvant chemotherapy, preoperative inferior vena cava filter placement when technically feasible, and repeat imaging to reassess the resectability of both the primary tumor and VTT. Surgery was undertaken only when both lesions were considered resectable. VTT involving peripheral venous branches or completely occluded and enlarged major veins was managed with en bloc venous resection, whereas thrombectomy was performed for VTT involving patent or partially patent major veins. Postoperative chemotherapy was initiated 2 to 3 weeks after surgery. After excluding one patient without pathologic confirmation of the macroscopic VTT, two patients in whom en bloc resection of the primary tumor was not achieved, and seven patients who did not receive postoperative chemotherapy, 29 patients were included in this retrospective analysis. The study population was young (mean ± SD age 16 ± 7 years), with a slight male predominance (17 of 29 patients), and primary tumors were distributed between the extremities (16 of 29) and pelvis (13 of 29). More than half of the patients presented with metastatic disease (16 of 29), most VTTs involved major venous trunks (22 of 29), and 20 of 29 patients had < 90% tumor necrosis after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. Given the high risk of early progression in these patients, progression-free survival (PFS) was selected as the primary endpoint. Secondary endpoints included overall survival (OS), local recurrence-free survival (LRFS), and metastasis PFS (MPFS). Results Patients treated under the standardized algorithm had limited durable disease control, with disease progression in 26 of 29 patients, a median PFS of 7 months (95% confidence interval [CI] 0 to 16), and an estimated 2-year OS of 60%. Patients with localized disease had longer PFS (median 13 months [95% CI 8 to 19] versus 5 months [95% CI 4 to 5]; p = 0.046) and MPFS (median 13 months [95% CI 8 to 19] versus 4.6 months [95% CI 4 to 5]; p = 0.04) than those with metastatic disease. There were no differences in OS (not reached versus median 32 months [95% CI 10 to 54]; p = 0.52), PFS (median 11 months [95% CI 0 to 31] versus 6 months [95% CI 3 to 9]; p = 0.62), LRFS (median 21 months [95% CI 9 to 34] versus 61 months [95% CI 2 to 120]; p = 0.54), and MPFS (median 13 months [95% CI 0.3 to 25] versus 8 months [95% CI 3 to 13]; p = 0.24) between patients who had thrombectomy versus en bloc venous resection. Conclusion Despite a standardized multidisciplinary approach incorporating perioperative chemotherapy and aggressive resection of both the primary tumor and macroscopic VTT, progression remained frequent, and durable disease control was uncommon. Among these 29 selected patients, VTT resection strategy-thrombectomy versus en bloc venous resection-was not detectably associated with oncologic outcomes, although the two groups were not directly comparable. Surgeons should recognize that osteosarcoma with macroscopic VTT is a rare, highly aggressive condition for which current treatment modalities seldom achieve a cure and should carefully balance the potential oncologic benefit of aggressive surgery against its morbidity. Future prospective multicenter studies should refine patient-level selection criteria and directly evaluate the incorporation of adjuvant radiotherapy into this standardized treatment algorithm. Novel systemic therapies should also be investigated to improve control of metastatic and rapidly progressive disease. Level of evidence Level III, therapeutic study.

title: How Much Do Horizontally Referenced and Interteardrop-referenced Acetabular Coverage Indices Differ During Standing in Adults With Hip Pain?
abstract: Background Acetabular coverage is conventionally assessed using the lateral center-edge angle (LCEA) and acetabular index. However, on standing radiographs, these measurements may be referenced either to the pelvis or to the weightbearing horizontal. Whether selection of these reference lines leads to clinically relevant differences in acetabular coverage interpretation is uncertain. Questions/purposes (1) How do horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced LCEA and acetabular index measurements compare in patients with nonarthritic hip pain? (2) How are the magnitude and direction of pelvic obliquity associated with differences between horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced acetabular coverage measurements? (3) What are the magnitude and direction of pelvic obliquity in young adults undergoing assessment for unilateral nonarthritic hip pain? (4) How are hip-length discrepancy measures based on the lesser trochanter and hip center of rotation associated with the magnitude and direction of pelvic obliquity? Methods In this retrospective comparative study, 598 patients evaluated at a tertiary-referral young-adult hip clinic between June 2021 and June 2025 were identified; 10% (60 of 598) were excluded for bilateral hip involvement or prior procedures, 5% (28 of 598) for insufficient radiographs, and 3% (17 of 598) for age 50 years or older, leaving 493 patients age 16 to 49 years with unilateral nonarthritic hip conditions and standing AP pelvic radiographs to be included. The mean ± SD age was 35 ± 8 years; 39% (191 of 493) were male. Diagnoses included dysplasia; cam-type, mixed, and pincer-type femoroacetabular impingement; isolated labral tears; and other nonarthritic hip conditions. In each hip, LCEA and acetabular index were measured using horizontal and interteardrop-referenced measurements, and classification disagreement was assessed using LCEA (< 20°, 20° to 25°, 25° to 40°, > 40°) and acetabular index (< 0°, 0° to 10°, > 10°) categories. Associations between pelvic obliquity magnitude and measurement-difference magnitude were assessed using linear regression, with directional relationships assessed graphically. Pelvic obliquity was measured as the angle between the interteardrop and horizontal reference lines, with direction defined relative to the clinically evaluated side. Hip-length discrepancy measures based on the lesser trochanter and hip center of rotation were compared across pelvic obliquity magnitude and direction groups. After interrater standardization, each patient was randomly allocated to one of two observers, who performed all measurements for that patient; a third observer reviewed a random sample. Interobserver intraclass correlation coefficients ranged from 0.69 to 0.87. Results Mean ± SD absolute differences between horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced measurements were 2° ± 1° for both LCEA and acetabular index. Classification disagreement occurred in 14% (69 of 493) using LCEA-based categories and 10% (51 of 493) using acetabular index-based categories, most notably when interteardrop-referenced LCEA indicated borderline dysplasia and horizontally referenced LCEA indicated normal coverage (29% [28 of 95]). Each 1° increase in pelvic obliquity magnitude was associated with an approximately 1° greater measurement difference for LCEA (β = 0.89 [95% confidence interval (CI) 0.86 to 0.93]; R2 = 0.86; p < 0.001) and acetabular index (β = 0.90 [95% CI 0.87 to 0.93]; R2 = 0.88; p < 0.001). Mean absolute pelvic obliquity magnitude was 2° ± 1°; 40% (197 of 493) had pelvic obliquity of 2° to < 5° and 3% (14 of 493) had pelvic obliquity ≥ 5°. The clinically evaluated hemipelvis was abducted in 44% (218 of 493), adducted in 39% (192 of 493), and neutral in 17% (83 of 493). Lesser trochanter-based hip-length discrepancy was 2 ± 2 mm with a neutral pelvis, 3 ± 3 mm with abduction, and 4 ± 3 mm with adduction (p < 0.001), and increased from 3 ± 3 mm to 5 ± 3 mm and 7 ± 3 mm across increasing pelvic obliquity magnitude categories (p < 0.001). Hip center of rotation-based values were 2 ± 2 mm in all three direction groups (p = 0.03) and 2 ± 2 mm, 3 ± 2 mm, and 3 ± 3 mm across increasing magnitude categories (p = 0.22). Conclusion These findings indicate that horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced measurements can yield discordant acetabular coverage estimates and radiographic classifications for the same patient. As standing radiographs become more widely incorporated into hip evaluation, comparison of horizontally referenced and interteardrop-referenced LCEA and acetabular index measurements may provide additional information by revealing pelvic-obliquity-associated differences in measured coverage while standing. In patients with appreciable pelvic obliquity, these differences may warrant consideration when interpreting acetabular morphology and discussing the relative indications for treatment or procedural options because they may lead clinicians to disagree about whether the same hip meets thresholds used in treatment planning. Future work should correlate measurements based on horizontal referencing and interteardrop referencing in patients with appreciable pelvic obliquity with clinical and surgical outcomes to (1) determine whether acetabular indices measured using the interteardrop line or floor-based horizontal reference confer superior clinical value and (2) define procedure-specific thresholds for relevant diagnostic subgroups. Level of evidence Level III, diagnostic study.

title: What Are the Long-term Outcomes of Periacetabular Osteotomy in a United States Cohort?
abstract: Background Periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) is an effective and common hip-preserving procedure used to treat symptomatic acetabular dysplasia of the hip. Evidence regarding long-term outcomes after PAO remains limited. Information regarding long-term outcomes may be important in developing reasonable expectations for both patients and surgeons to facilitate effective therapeutic decision-making. Questions/purposes (1) What is the likelihood of long-term hip preservation and the level of pain at a minimum of 25 years of follow-up after PAO? (2) What clinical and radiographic factors were associated with patients having a poor result, which we defined either as having THA or a WOMAC score of ≥ 10 points at the most recent survey? (3) What were the outcome scores of patients who underwent THA after PAO, and how did these scores compare to the scores of the preserved hips and to the scores of age-related norms? Methods We retrospectively evaluated the cohort of the first 142 patients (171 hips) who underwent PAO performed by one surgeon to treat symptomatic dysplasia between 1991 and 1998. Twenty-three percent (33 of 142) of patients (37 hips) were lost to follow-up. This included six patients (6 hips) who had died, 23 patients (26 hips) who could not be located, and four patients (5 hips) who did not complete questionnaires. Seventy-seven percent (109 of 142) of eligible patients (134 hips) returned complete questionnaires at a median (range) of 27 years (25 to 33) after PAO. Our analyzed group included 87% female patients (95 patients, 117 hips) and 13% male patients (14 patients, 17 hips). The median (range) age at surgery was 25 years (9 to 45). The median (range) time of review after PAO was 27 years (25 to 33). The 53 hips that had undergone THA were reviewed at a median (range) of 11 years (1 to 28) after the THA. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to assess survivorship free from conversion to THA. Hips were postoperatively evaluated using the pain subscale of the WOMAC index. We characterized a poor clinical outcome as either having a preserved hip with a WOMAC pain score of ≥ 10 or undergoing THA. All patients who were analyzed returned questionnaires; some were seen in person with images. Factors associated with a patient having a high (poor) WOMAC score for pain or undergoing THA were evaluated using a multinomial logistic regression model using generalized estimating equations. Results Of patients analyzed, 60% (81 of 134) of hips remained preserved. Forty percent (53 of 134) of hips had undergone THA at a median of 22 years after PAO. The survivorship free from conversion to THA at 25 years after PAO was 70% (95% confidence interval [CI] 62% to 78%), and the median (range) level of pain was 1 (0 to 20) of 20 points. After controlling for potentially confounding variables including sex, preoperative lateral center-edge angle and anterior center-edge angle, and postoperative lateral center-edge angle, we found that the following factors were associated with increased odds of having either a poor (≥ 10 points) WOMAC pain score or conversion to THA: preoperative joint space width ≤ 2 mm (HR 7.3 [95% CI 2.8 to 19.2]), labral tear noted intraoperatively (HR 2.8 [95% CI 1.3 to 5.8]), age at surgery > 21 years and < 35 years (HR 2.6 [95% CI 1.1 to 5.9]), and age at surgery ≥ 35 years (HR 3.4 [95% CI 1.1 to 11.0]). In patients who underwent THA, the median (range) WOMAC score was 1 (0 to 20) (lower scores represent less pain and better function), the median (range) modified Harris hip score was 85 (7 to 91) points (higher scores represent less pain and better function), and the median (range) HOOS pain score was 95 (0 to 100). The mean University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) activity level score for the THA group was 6. In general, these scores did not differ by clinically important margins when compared with the hips that had not undergone THA or compared with age-related score norms. Conclusion While a majority of hips can be preserved with good function at a mean of 27 years after PAO, our findings suggest that surgery should be considered as soon as the diagnosis of symptomatic dysplasia is made, given that older age at the time of surgery was independently associated with later THA or a WOMAC pain score of ≥ 10. If a patient develops painful arthrosis after a PAO, THA should be offered and expected to provide function comparable to age-related norms. Prospective registry-based multicenter studies of patients treated for symptomatic hip dysplasia are indicated to improve outcomes. Level of evidence level III, therapeutic study.

In patients who underwent THA, the median (range) WOMAC score was 1 (0 to 20) (lower scores represent less pain and better function), the median (range) modified Harris hip score was 85 (7 to 91) points (higher scores represent less pain and better function), and the median (range) HOOS pain score was 95 (0 to 100). The mean University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) activity level score for the THA group was 6. In general, these scores did not differ by clinically important margins when compared with the hips that had not undergone THA or compared with age-related score norms.

Conclusion

While a majority of hips can be preserved with good function at a mean of 27 years after PAO, our findings suggest that surgery should be considered as soon as the diagnosis of symptomatic dysplasia is made, given that older age at the time of surgery was independently associated with later THA or a WOMAC pain score of ≥ 10. If a patient develops painful arthrosis after a PAO, THA should be offered and expected to provide function comparable to age-related norms. Prospective registry-based multicenter studies of patients treated for symptomatic hip dysplasia are indicated to improve outcomes.

Level of evidence level

III, therapeutic study.

title: Combination Therapy of Injectables With Energy-Based Treatments for Facial Rejuvenation: An Updated Review.
abstract: Background Fillers are frequently combined with other injectables and energy-based devices to target volume loss, dynamic rhytides, and photodamage. Questions remain regarding optimal treatment sequencing, safety, and synergistic clinical efficacy.OBJECTIVETo evalute the current evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of combining injectable therapies with energy-based treatments for facial rejuvenation. Methods MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus were searched using keywords on dermal fillers with neuromodulators, intense pulsed light (IPL), laser, microfocused ultrasound with visualization (MFU-V), high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU), or radiofrequency (RF). Studies reporting safety, efficacy, sequencing, or clinical outcomes were included. Results Combining fillers with neuromodulators produces synergistic improvements in facial rejuvenation by addressing volume loss and muscular hyperactivity with superior outcomes and longer treatment durability compared with monotherapy. Intense pulsed light, nonablative lasers, MFU-V, HIFU, and RF appear safe when used with fillers, with studies demonstrating no significant adverse interactions or compromise of filler integrity. Combination treatment may enhance optimize facial contouring, improve skin quality, and improve patient satisfaction and retention. Histologic and clinical studies suggest synergistic effects when MFU-V/RF are combined with biostimulatory fillers. Conclusion Combination treatment with fillers and complementary modalities offers a comprehensive approach to facial rejuvenation. Current evidence supports the safety of most nonablative combination protocols. Additional studies are needed to assess the safety and efficacy of combining fillers with more aggressive resurfacing procedures and novel devices.

title: Intramuscular Well-differentiated Liposarcoma of the Brachioradialis Muscle.
abstract: Tumors of the brachioradialis muscle are rare, with only a few case reports including synovial sarcoma, fibrohistiocytoma and a benign lipoma. An intramuscular well-differentiated liposarcoma of the brachioradialis muscle is herein presented. A 44-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of a slow-growing mass in the region of the brachioradialis muscle of the forearm, which did not directly involve any adjacent structures but was abutting the radial neurovascular bundle. The mass was bilobular with the larger portion being a benign lipoma with a deep component which was confirmed by immunohistochemistry to be a well-differentiated liposarcoma with no features of dedifferentiation. The tumor revealed spindle cells with retained expression of RB1, negative for desmin and CD34 and was fluorescence in situ hybridization positive with MDM2 amplification. The patient had a successful resection with clear margins and preservation of the radial neurovascular bundle that abutted the deep margin of the brachioradialis muscle. There was no neurovascular deficit or disability postoperatively. On 2-year follow-up after local radiotherapy the patient remains tumor free with no signs of recurrence or metastases on computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging. Well-differentiated intramuscular liposarcoma of the brachioradialis has not been documented based on our PubMed literature search. This case demonstrates a technique with preservation of forearm function coupled with recommendations for focused external beam radiotherapy. A multidisciplinary approach is essential, involving surgeons, pathologists, radiologists and oncologists. Accurate diagnosis relies on the integration of clinical, radiologic, and pathologic data, as well as thorough sampling of the tumor through excision biopsy.

title: Novel markers for atrial substrate characterization: implications on atrial fibrillation risk stratification.
abstract: Purpose of review Atrial fibrillation is increasingly recognized as a manifestation of an underlying atrial disease process that is incompletely captured by conventional temporal classification. This review examines established and emerging markers of atrial substrate and their potential role in atrial fibrillation risk stratification. Recent findings Electrocardiographic indices, left atrial volumetric and strain measures, computed tomography-derived left atrial wall characteristics, late gadolinium enhancement and flow assessment by cardiac magnetic resonance, high-density electroanatomic mapping, circulating biomarkers and genetic profiling provide complementary measures of electrical, structural, mechanical and hemodynamic remodelling. Recent studies have refined noninvasive identification of low-voltage substrate and risk stratification of atrial fibrillation progression and complications, evaluated substrate-guided ablation strategies, and expanded understanding of the prognostic significance of emerging substrate markers. Summary Multimodal atrial substrate characterization may improve prediction of atrial fibrillation onset and progression, thromboembolic complications and outcomes after rhythm-control therapy. Clinical translation requires standardized acquisition and analytical methods, reproducible thresholds, prospective validation of integrated risk models, and prospective trials demonstrating improved outcomes with substrate-guided management.

title: Advanced coronary computed tomography angiography plaque phenotyping for precision prevention.
abstract: Purpose of review In this review, we outline the role coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) plays in the diagnosis of coronary artery disease (CAD) and in facilitating risk assessment. Plaque quantification and phenotyping using CCTA is a promising approach in guiding cardiovascular preventive management. Recent findings There is growing interest in how artificial intelligence-based quantitative plaque analysis using CCTA (AI-CPA) can guide preventive therapy. The review summarizes studies that show prognostic utility of CCTA-derived plaque quantification and phenotyping as well as outlines more recent studies that show the impact of AI-CPA in patient management decisions, allowing a more individualized approach to preventive strategies. Summary CCTA provides a comprehensive assessment extending beyond coronary luminal stenosis to include plaque quantification, plaque phenotyping, functional assessment of stenotic lesions and vascular inflammation, further refining traditional approaches of risk prediction.In summary, the growing evidence highlights the importance of incorporating CCTA-based plaque volume and plaque phenotype analysis in better informing physicians about individual's risk and in guiding preventive management.

title: MRI-based biomarkers for risk stratification and assessment of treatment response in Metabolic dysfunction-associated Steatotic liver disease.
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) affects up to 38% of the population globally. Liver biopsy, the historical reference standard, is invasive, subject to sampling error and not scalable. MRI-based biomarkers provide non-invasive, quantitative whole liver assessment. MRI proton density fat fraction (MRI-PDFF) is the most accurate noninvasive measure of steatosis (thresholds of 6.4%, 17.4% and 22.1% for grades ≥1, ≥2 and 3), and a ≥30% relative reduction is associated with histologic response. Liver stiffness by magnetic resonance elastography (MRE-LS) is the most accurate imaging biomarker for fibrosis: MRE-LS of 3.1-4.4 kPa corresponds to F2-F3 and ≥5 kPa to cirrhosis, and each 1-kPa increase is associated with a 43% higher risk of hepatic decompensation. Iron-corrected T1 is a sensitive but nonspecific marker of disease activity whose prognostic value requires further study. Composite scores, MAST, MEFIB, and MASH Resolution Index, combine imaging and blood tests for advanced fibrosis diagnosis and response assessment. MRE is cost-effective compared with vibration-controlled transient elastography for detecting advanced fibrosis. Artificial intelligence may broaden access by automating analysis and enabling PDFF from routine MRI. We review the evidence supporting these biomarkers for diagnosis, prognosis and regulatory use, and their role in clinical trials and in treatment decisions for approved MASH therapies.

title: Repeated Exposure to Military Low-Level Blast Is Associated With Regionally Specific Reductions in Gray Matter Volume in Breachers and Snipers.
abstract: Objective To examine the association between duration of repeated exposure to low-level blast and alteration in brain structure. Setting Data were collected at 2 neuroimaging facilities. Participants Canadian Armed Forces breachers ( n = 30) and snipers ( n = 31) with a history of repeated exposure to low-level blast (average years = 9.70, SD = 4.57) and sex- and age-matched active military controls ( n = 57). Design MRI and neurocognitive data from breachers and snipers were collected prospectively at baseline (time 1) and after a training exercise involving a concentrated regimen of blast exposure (time 2) (time gap = 80.56 days, SD = 36.90). Time 1 and time 2 data were used to assess the chronic and training-related effects of blast exposure, respectively. MRI and neurocognitive data from controls were collected twice with a comparable time gap. Main measures High-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans, plus neurocognitive measures. Results Voxel-based morphometry conducted on MRI data collected at time 1 demonstrated that compared with controls, there was lower regional gray matter volume in left inferior frontal gyrus in snipers, and bilaterally in parahippocampal gyrus (bordering on amygdala) in breachers. Regional gray matter volume in left inferior frontal gyrus in snipers predicted neurocognitive function. We did not observe any difference in regional white matter volume between groups at time 1, nor any changes in regional gray or white matter volume between time 1 and time 2. Conclusion Chronic but not training-related low-level blast exposure was associated with dissociable patterns of regional gray matter volume reduction in snipers and breachers, and regional gray matter volume predicted neurocognitive function in snipers. The differential pattern of structural alteration between breachers and snipers and its relationship with neurocognitive function in snipers can inform health monitoring programs for diagnosis and treatment of blast-exposed service members and Veterans.

title: Structure-Function Correlates of Radiation Chorioretinopathy: Insights from Microperimetry and Swept-Source OCTA.
abstract: Purpose To investigate optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) alterations and structure-function relationships in radiation chorioretinopathy (RCR) following external beam radiotherapy for choroidal melanoma. Methods Cross-sectional, case-control study including 21 eyes with RCR treated with CyberKnife (CK) or proton beam therapy (PBT), and 21 healthy fellow eyes as controls. Participants underwent swept-source 6×6-mm OCTA, spectral-domain OCT, and 68-stimulus mesopic microperimetry. OCTA metrics included vessel density (VD) of superficial (SCP) and deep capillary plexuses (DCP), foveal avascular zone (FAZ) area, and choriocapillaris flow-deficit percentage (CCFD%). Retinal thickness and functional outcomes-including best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) and mesopic retinal sensitivity (RS)-were analyzed within predefined regions. Generalized linear mixed-effects regression models assessed group differences and structure-function associations. Results Compared with controls, irradiated eyes demonstrated significantly reduced SCP and DCP VD, enlarged FAZ, and increased CCFD% across all macular regions (all p<0.001), despite preserved retinal thickness. Both BCVA and mesopic RS were significantly reduced in irradiated eyes (p<0.001), with no significant differences between CK- and PBT-treated eyes. In multivariable models, DCP VD within the 5-mm circle (p<0.01), CCFD% within the 3-5-mm ring (p<0.001), and parafoveal retinal thickness (p<0.05) were the strongest independent predictors of mesopic RS (adjusted R2=0.73). No biomarker was independently associated with BCVA (adjusted R2=0.44). Conclusions RCR is characterized by diffuse retinal and choriocapillaris microvascular impairment that correlates strongly with mesopic RS but not with BCVA. Microperimetry outperformed BCVA in detecting functional consequences of radiation-induced neurovascular damage, supporting the role of OCTA-derived metrics as relevant biomarkers for RCR diagnosis and monitoring.

title: Visual outcomes and intraocular lens selection in highly myopic eyes.
abstract: Purpose of review To synthesize recent evidence on visual prognosis and intraocular lens (IOL) selection in highly myopic eyes undergoing cataract surgery, with emphasis on retinal phenotyping, optical biometry and IOL power calculation, capsular-zonular stability, and the use of toric and presbyopia-correcting IOLs. Recent findings Swept-source optical biometry and newer-generation formulas have improved refractive predictability but have not eliminated error in eyes with extreme axial length or low-, zero-, and negative-power IOLs. Macular optical coherence tomography (OCT) has become central to estimating visual potential because pathologic myopia and subtle outer retinal or tractional abnormalities may constrain postoperative acuity and contrast sensitivity. High myopia alone is not an absolute contraindication to toric or presbyopia-correcting IOLs; however, candidacy should be determined by macular function, capsular stability, and the patient's tolerance for dysphotopsia and residual refractive error. Capsular tension rings appear most useful in selected eyes with axial length ≥30 mm or positioning-sensitive IOLs rather than as a routine intervention. IOL material also warrants consideration because hydrophobic acrylic lenses may reduce long-term posterior capsule opacification in highly myopic eyes. Summary Cataract surgery in high myopia requires phenotype-based planning rather than axial-length-driven lens selection. The most durable strategy integrates validated biometry, macular structure and function, capsular-zonular anatomy, realistic refractive goals, and continued retinal surveillance.

title: Recent advances in optical coherence tomography for glaucoma: from macular imaging and optical coherence tomography angiography to artificial intelligence and portable platforms.
abstract: Purpose of review Recent advances are extending optical coherence tomography (OCT)'s role beyond conventional structural metrics. This review summarizes recent developments in macular OCT, OCT angiography (OCTA), artificial intelligence (AI), and portable/home-based OCT. Recent findings Macular ganglion-cell measures (ganglion-cell-inner plexiform layer, ganglion cell complex) increasingly complement retinal nerve fiber layer assessment, offering greater diagnostic/prognostic value in advanced glaucoma, myopia, and certain glaucoma subtypes. OCTA is emerging as a complementary vascular biomarker; peripapillary vessel density shows the most consistent link to progression, with early evidence that vascular changes may precede detectable structural or functional decline. Deep learning models increasingly use raw or multimodal imaging rather than summary parameters; foundation and multimodal architectures (e.g., RETFound-based) show strong diagnostic performance and improved generalizability across demographics and disease severity. However, AI-based progression prediction remains less robust than cross-sectional diagnosis, especially under external validation. Portable/home-based OCT may extend monitoring beyond the clinic, though clinical utility remains investigational. Summary The field is moving toward multimodal, longitudinal, AI-supported glaucoma assessment integrating structural, vascular, and functional biomarkers rather than interpreting them in isolation. Key priorities for translation include standardized acquisition and analysis across devices, large and diverse external validation cohorts, interpretable models, and evidence that AI and remote imaging improve clinically meaningful outcomes. These developments should make OCT increasingly central to earlier detection and individualized monitoring of glaucoma, but none currently replace established structural and functional assessment or clinical judgment.

originalAbstract:
Purpose of review

Recent advances are extending optical coherence tomography (OCT)'s role beyond conventional structural metrics. This review summarizes recent developments in macular OCT, OCT angiography (OCTA), artificial intelligence (AI), and portable/home-based OCT.

Recent findings

Macular ganglion-cell measures (ganglion-cell-inner plexiform layer, ganglion cell complex) increasingly complement retinal nerve fiber layer assessment, offering greater diagnostic/prognostic value in advanced glaucoma, myopia, and certain glaucoma subtypes. OCTA is emerging as a complementary vascular biomarker; peripapillary vessel density shows the most consistent link to progression, with early evidence that vascular changes may precede detectable structural or functional decline. Deep learning models increasingly use raw or multimodal imaging rather than summary parameters; foundation and multimodal architectures (e.g., RETFound-based) show strong diagnostic performance and improved generalizability across demographics and disease severity. However, AI-based progression prediction remains less robust than cross-sectional diagnosis, especially under external validation. Portable/home-based OCT may extend monitoring beyond the clinic, though clinical utility remains investigational.

Summary

The field is moving toward multimodal, longitudinal, AI-supported glaucoma assessment integrating structural, vascular, and functional biomarkers rather than interpreting them in isolation. Key priorities for translation include standardized acquisition and analysis across devices, large and diverse external validation cohorts, interpretable models, and evidence that AI and remote imaging improve clinically meaningful outcomes. These developments should make OCT increasingly central to earlier detection and individualized monitoring of glaucoma, but none currently replace established structural and functional assessment or clinical judgment.

title: Risk Factors for Normal-tension Glaucoma Progression: A Review.
abstract: This review identified disc hemorrhages, intraocular pressure variability, and systemic vascular dysregulation as consistent predictors of normal-tension glaucoma progression, highlighting the need for risk stratification to guide individualized treatment, follow-up, and prognosis. Normal-tension glaucoma (NTG) is characterized by progressive optic neuropathy despite intraocular pressure (IOP) consistently within the conventionally defined normal limits. While some patients remain stable without treatment, others progress rapidly to irreversible vision loss. This review summarizes current evidence on predictive factors for NTG progression to support future risk stratification tools that aid clinical decision-making and prognosis. A comprehensive search of PubMed, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO ICTRP identified studies published between 2015 and 2025. Eligible studies included meta-analyses, clinical trials, cohort studies, case-control studies, and case series evaluating predictive factors for NTG onset or progression. Forty-five studies met inclusion criteria. Reported predictors include clinical biomarkers (female sex, younger age, labile IOP), imaging structural biomarkers (retinal nerve fibre layer thinning, macular ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer loss), corneal biomechanics (low corneal hysteresis, high deformability), optic disc morphology (tilted discs, lamina cribrosa defects, disc haemorrhages), systemic/vascular factors (nocturnal hypotension, ocular perfusion pressure variability, migraine, Raynaud's phenomenon, obstructive sleep apnoea), and genetic predispositions. NTG progression results from IOP-dependent and IOP-independent mechanisms. Among predictors, disc haemorrhages, IOP variability, and systemic vascular dysregulation emerge as the most consistent indicators of progression. Identifying at-risk patients is essential for tailoring treatment and follow-up, preventing overtreatment in stable cases, and avoiding irreversible sight loss. Future research could establish practical prognostic tools based on the most influential risk factors.

title: Nasal Dermoid Cysts Mimicking Lacrimal and Periorbital Infections in Children: A Clinicoradiologic Case Series.
abstract: Nasal dermoids, also referred to as nasal dermoid sinus cysts, and the more cranially located nasofrontal dermoid cysts may present with pediatric periorbital inflammation or masquerade as lacrimal excretory system infections, delaying definitive diagnosis and proper management. We describe 6 children (5 boys, 1 girl; age range, 12 months-48 months) who presented with upper eyelid abscesses, draining periocular sinuses, or dacryocystitis-like swelling secondary to nasal dermoid sinus cyst or nasofrontal dermoid cyst. All had received repeated courses of systemic antibiotics before formal diagnosis; 4 had undergone incision and drainage, and 1 had undergone prior nasolacrimal probing before the definitive diagnosis was established. A midline nasal pit or sinus was identified in all patients. CT demonstrated characteristic osseous abnormalities, and MRI better delineated tract extent and assessed intracranial involvement in 4 patients. Four patients underwent complete surgical excision, with no recurrence of infection over a follow-up period ranging from 1 to 4 years. Nasal dermoids should be considered in young children with recurrent or atypical periorbital inflammation. Careful nasal midline examination and cross-sectional imaging can prevent misdiagnosis and facilitate timely definitive management.

title: From imaging to intelligence: AI applications in CT and MRI for hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, largely due to high recurrence rates after curative treatment and poor prognosis in advanced-stage disease. Multiphasic computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) play central roles in the noninvasive diagnosis and management of HCC; however, diagnostic variability and limited sensitivity for early-stage and atypical lesions continue to pose major clinical challenges. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful tool for enhancing medical image analysis and improving clinical decision-making in liver oncology. This review summarizes recent advances in AI-based applications for HCC imaging using CT and MRI. We discuss the roles of AI in lesion detection and segmentation, differential diagnosis and tumor classification, imaging-based biological characterization, and prediction of treatment response and prognosis. In particular, radiomics and deep learning approaches have enabled automated extraction of high-dimensional imaging features, facilitating noninvasive assessment of tumor aggressiveness and heterogeneity. The integration of multimodal data, including imaging, clinical, and molecular information, further enhances predictive performance and personalized risk stratification. Despite encouraging results, most existing studies are limited by retrospective designs, heterogeneous methodologies, and insufficient external validation. Challenges related to model interpretability, data standardization, and clinical integration also remain unresolved. We highlight current limitations and future research directions, emphasizing the need for multi-center collaboration, prospective validation, and development of transparent and regulatory-compliant systems. With continued technological innovation and interdisciplinary collaboration, AI-driven imaging analysis is expected to play an increasingly important role in precision medicine and outcome optimization for patients with HCC.

title: In Vivo Detection of Ampullary T2 Hypointensity as a Marker of Vestibular Atelectasis.
abstract: Background and purpose Vestibular atelectasis (VA) is a histologically defined collapse of the membranous labyrinth, often accompanied by dense basophilic deposits. While delayed postcontrast 3D-FLAIR imaging allows indirect visualization of VA, no in vivo correlate of the basophilic deposits has been reported. This study describes a novel T2-weighted hypointense signal within the ampullae and utricle as a potential imaging biomarker of VA and explores its clinical relevance in patients with bilateral vestibular areflexia. Materials and methods This retrospective study included 47 patients with bilateral vestibular areflexia, confirmed by video Head Impulse Test and vestibular-evoked myogenic potentials. All underwent 3T MRI with delayed postcontrast 3D-FLAIR and high-resolution T2-weighted sequences. The presence and distribution of ampullary or utricular T2 hypointensities were evaluated and correlated with radiological VA, clinical presentation, and vestibular function. Results Among the 47 patients included, VA was identified in 32 (68.1%). A distinct T2 hypointense signal was observed in 25 patients (53.2%), exclusively within the VA group. These hypointensities were significantly more prevalent in the superior and posterior ampullae compared to the lateral (FDR-P<0.001). VA patients were significantly younger, had better hearing thresholds and more severe posterior canal dysfunction; short vertigo episodes were more frequent in this group without reaching statistical significance. In age-adjusted Firth logistic regression, ampullary hypointensity was the only variable independently associated with VA (odds ratio: 124.59, 95% CI: 5.35-2900.22; apparent area under the curve: 0.973, 95% CI: 0.890-0.994), although the estimate was imprecise owing to quasi-complete separation (FDR-P=0.0104). Conclusion A T2 hypointense signal within the ampullae and utricle was observed exclusively in patients with radiological vestibular atelectasis in this cohort. Its anatomical distribution is compatible with the basophilic deposits described in histopathological series, although this correspondence remains hypothetical in the absence of tissue analysis. This MRI sign may raise suspicion of VA when delayed postcontrast 3D-FLAIR imaging is unavailable or contraindicated, rather than replace it.

title: Assessment of Magnetic Resonance Imaging-Derived Synthetic Computed Tomography for Otologic Surgical Planning.
abstract: Synthetic computed tomography (sCT) techniques generate CT-equivalent images from magnetic resonance imaging to support surgical planning while reducing radiation exposure. Although prior work shows strong quantitative agreement between sCT and real CT (rCT), its clinical validity for otologic surgical planning remains uncertain. Cross-sectional reader study. Academic tertiary medical center. Otolaryngologists and neuroradiologists. Participants reviewed 60 CT images (30 rCT, 30 sCT) and classified each as real or synthetic, while assessing acceptability for surgical planning. Paired rCT-sCT images were reviewed side-by-side to identify image type and evaluate potential limitations of sCT for clinical use. Accuracy of distinguishing sCT from rCT; acceptability of sCT for cochlear implant and middle ear surgical planning; qualitative assessment of anatomic discrepancies. Nine readers participated. In single-image review, overall discrimination of sCT from rCT was limited, with mean accuracy of 57.2 ± 7.1% among otolaryngologists and 77.8 ± 1.0% among neuroradiologists (area under the curve: 0.60 ± 0.10 vs. 0.80 ± 0.01, P < 0.001). Acceptability ratings for cochlear implant planning were high for both rCT (97.8% to 98.9%) and sCT (90.0% to 93.9%), with similar findings for middle ear surgery (rCT 92.2% to 97.8%, sCT 86.7% to 87.8%). Concern regarding sCT reliability was reported in ∼20% of cases and primarily involved ossicular morphology, mastoid air cell architecture, and postoperative anatomy. This exploratory study suggests that sCT can approximate rCT for otologic surgical planning in cases with preserved anatomy, with high reported acceptability ratings across specialties. However, discrepancies identified in a subset of cases suggest that further validation is needed to define its role in clinical practice.

title: Optimizing Jugular Paraganglioma Management Using Preoperative 3D Volumetric Analysis.
abstract: Determine optimal management of jugular paragangliomas (JPs) based on preoperative tumor volume. Retrospective review of patients undergoing surgery for JPs from January 2008 to March 2023. Tertiary care center. Adult patients with surgically treated JPs and available preoperative imaging, cranial nerve data, and follow-up were analyzed. Treatment decisions, including near-total resection (NTR) or subtotal resection (STR) with adjuvant radiation, were based on tumor size, location, and patient-specific risk factors. Preoperative tumor volumes were measured using standardized 3D MRI analysis. Thirty-eight patients underwent JP surgery. Greater total tumor volume correlated with receipt of postoperative radiation therapy (RT) (median 5.4 cm3 with RT vs. 3.8 cm3 without, P=0.034). An anterior-medial volume >2 cm3 was strongly correlated with receipt of adjuvant RT (P=0.006), suggesting that tumors with larger anterior-medial extensions are more likely to be managed with adjuvant therapy. Higher total tumor volume was significantly associated with new postoperative lower cranial nerve deficits (P=0.021), whereas greater anterior tumor volume analyzed as a continuous variable was not (P=0.331). Preoperative volumetric analysis can guide JP management, particularly for tumors with high anterior-medial volume, where STR with adjuvant radiation may help preserve lower cranial nerve function. Violation of the jugular bulb's medial wall remains the sine qua non for postoperative cranial nerve dysfunction, underscoring the importance of precise preoperative planning. Despite its retrospective design and sample size, this framework supports a more conservative, volume-informed surgical approach.

title: Perioperative hemodynamic optimization.
abstract: Perioperative hemodynamic optimization using goal-directed therapy (GDT) reduces complications and mortality in high-risk surgery. This review synthesizes advances over the last few years, focusing on dynamic physiological targets, predictive artificial intelligence, microcirculatory and endothelial protection, individualized arterial pressure targets, volume stewardship and novel nonadrenergic rescue vasopressors for postcardiopulmonary bypass vasoplegia, and extracorporeal blood purification for refractory vasoplegia in surgical sepsis. Clinical practice has shifted from rigid volumetric protocols toward individualized physiological stewardship and endothelial glycocalyx preservation, framed within the four-phase dynamic continuum (ROSE concept: Resuscitation, Optimization, Stabilization, and Evacuation). Machine-learning algorithms, such as the Hypotension Prediction Index, effectively preempt intraoperative hypotension. Point-of-care ultrasound protocols, notably the venous excess ultrasound (VExUS) score, prevent backward venous congestion. Concurrently, dynamic arterial elastance (Eadyn) distinguishes between vasodilation and preload deficit. In cardiothoracic surgery, postcardiopulmonary bypass vasoplegia mandates cautious fluid restriction and early multimodal nonadrenergic vasopressors, including methylene blue, hydroxocobalamin (vitamin B12), and synthetic angiotensin II, which effectively restore vascular tone and limit catecholamine toxicity. In surgical sepsis and refractory vasoplegic shock, blood purification therapies provide valuable hemodynamic rescue; the pioneer continuous hemodiafiltration with cytokine-adsorbing hemofilters (CAH-CHDF) and recent trial data with polymyxin B hemoperfusion (the TIGRIS trial) demonstrate significant vasopressor-sparing effects and restored vascular tone. Perioperative hemodynamic optimization has evolved into a multimodal, patient-tailored approach. Coupling dynamic fluid responsiveness with predictive monitoring, personalized blood pressure titration, nonadrenergic rescue for postbypass vasoplegic shock, organ venous congestion profiling, and extracorporeal humoral modulation provides comprehensive circulatory support while preventing fluid overload.

title: Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy Versus Image-Guided Gastrostomy Placement in Patients With Cirrhosis: A Multi-Institutional Research Network Study.
abstract: Background The selection of an appropriate technique for placement of a gastrostomy tube in patients with cirrhosis remains controversial due to concerns about adverse events. We used real-world data to compare outcomes after percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) versus fluoroscopically guided gastrostomy by an interventional radiologist (IR G-tube) in patients with cirrhosis. Methods We performed a multicenter retrospective cohort study of adults with cirrhosis who underwent gastrostomy tube placement from 2014 to 2023 using the TriNetX Research Network. Using relevant Current Procedural Terminology codes, patients were categorized into 2 groups: PEG (43246/0DH64UZ) or fluoroscopic IR G-tube (49440/0DH63UZ). Periprocedural adverse events were defined as short-term (14 d) or long-term (180 d). Propensity score matching was performed using demographic, clinical, and available laboratory covariates. Binary outcomes were reported as adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% CIs, whereas mortality was reported using adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) from Cox proportional hazards models. Survival was assessed with Kaplan-Meier analysis and log-rank testing. Results Of the 5028 patients meeting selection criteria, 1579 underwent PEG placement and 3449 underwent IR G-tube placement. Adjusted odds of periprocedural adverse events for PEG vs IR G-tube were as follows: aspiration pneumonia (aOR: 0.66, 95% CI: 0.51-0.85), hemorrhage (aOR: 0.79, CI: 0.59-1.06), blood transfusion (aOR: 0.99, CI: 0.78-1.27), and infection or peritonitis (aOR: 0.96, CI: 0.68-1.34). In the 6-month follow-up period, PEG placement was associated with lower odds of tube malfunction (aOR: 0.78, 95% CI: 0.64-0.96) and tube replacement (aOR: 0.47, 95% CI: 0.36-0.63). At 6 months, PEG placement was also associated with lower mortality risk (aHR: 0.80, 95% CI: 0.70-0.91; P=0.011). Conclusions In a large multicenter cohort of patients with cirrhosis, PEG and IR G-tube placement had similar short-term rates of bleeding and infectious adverse events, whereas PEG was associated with fewer tube malfunctions and replacements and lower observed mortality at 6 months.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Hepatology: Emerging Opportunities and Translational Challenges.
abstract: In December 2025, the Food and Drug Administration assessed and qualified the first artificial intelligence (AI)-powered tool for use in drug development trials; this AI system evaluates digital liver biopsies for steatohepatitis and fibrosis. However, AI is still being investigated before it can be applied directly to patient care in the field of Hepatology. Current patient-facing applications at most institutions are limited to assistive tools such as computer-aided polyp detection and large language model documentation tools that draft clinic notes and patient communications, although there exist radiographic and pathologic liver AI tools that could function at and may even exceed human capabilities. This review provides a broad introduction to AI and highlights clinical research that use AI to enhance the diagnosis, prognostication, and management of liver diseases. It will also discuss the challenges that will need to be overcome before AI can be adopted to clinical practice.

title: State of the art: thoracic ultrasound.
abstract: Purpose of review Thoracic ultrasound has continued to expand beyond simple bedside triage into a quantitative, procedure-guiding and increasingly artificial intelligence-augmented tool across pleural and respiratory medicine. This review summarizes the literature published over the past year, highlighting developments in effusion characterization, pneumothorax diagnosis, image-guided pleural procedures, artificial intelligence, training standards, critical care applications, malignant pleural effusion management, and diaphragm/interstitial lung disease assessment. Recent findings Elastography and contrast-enhanced ultrasound have moved from exploratory to comparative and multicentre randomized evaluation for effusion characterization and biopsy guidance. Meta-analyses have reaffirmed the superiority of point-of-care ultrasound over chest radiography for both pneumothorax and thoracentesis guidance. Artificial intelligence tools have shown that they can close the acquisition-skill gap for novice operators, although automated interpretation (particularly B-line quantification) remains inconsistent against expert consensus. A new UK national training standard for pleural procedures has been published, alongside the first validated thoracic-specific competency assessment tool. A large multicentre randomized trial found that a point-of-care ultrasound-driven diagnostic pathway did not improve early discharge rates in emergency department patients with dyspnoea, an important negative finding. Diaphragm and quantitative lung ultrasound continue to accumulate evidence as noninvasive markers of interstitial lung disease severity and ventilator weaning readiness. Summary The past year's literature confirms thoracic ultrasound's trajectory from a purely diagnostic adjunct towards a quantitative, procedure-integrated and artificial intelligence-supported modality, while also delivering important cautionary and negative findings that temper enthusiasm and clarify where evidence remains immature.

title: Clinical characteristics and prognostic implications of high-burden osteoarthritis in US adults: Evidence from NHANES 2011-2018.
abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is clinically heterogeneous. Most epidemiologic studies classify OA as present or absent based solely on self-report or radiographic criteria (binary diagnosis), which overlooks the wide variation in symptom burden and functional impact among individuals with OA. We aimed to define a high-burden OA phenotype in a nationally representative sample of US adults and to evaluate its clinical correlates and prognostic significance. This cross-sectional and longitudinal study used nationally representative National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2011-2018 data from adults aged ≥20 years, with mortality follow-up through the 2019 public-use Linked Mortality File. OA was defined by self-reported physician-diagnosed arthritis with self-classification as osteoarthritis/degenerative arthritis. High-burden OA was identified using work limitation, activity limitation, walking difficulty, need for special equipment, and difficulty with routine physical tasks. Conventional regression and survival analyses incorporated National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey sampling weights, strata, and primary sampling units. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), random forest, and extreme gradient boosting models were trained with sampling weights; held-out performance was additionally evaluated using survey-weighted metrics. Among 22,436 eligible adults, 14,772 were included in the complete-case analysis: 12,918 without OA, 662 with low-burden OA, and 1192 with high-burden OA. Most weighted baseline characteristics differed across the 3 groups (all P ≤ .005), whereas lifetime alcohol use did not (P = .568). Age- and sex-specific prevalence differed by age-group and sex (both P < .001), without evidence of an age-by-sex interaction (P = .395), and prevalence increased across body mass index categories (P for trend < 0.001). In weighted held-out evaluation, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator had the highest area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve (0.848), followed by random forest and XGBoost (both 0.839). Among 1853 participants in the OA survival cohort, 177 deaths occurred during a median observed follow-up of 4.58 years. High-burden OA was associated with all-cause mortality in the fully adjusted survey-weighted Cox model (hazard ratio 1.70, 95% confidence interval 1.08-2.68; P = .022). High-burden OA identifies a clinically vulnerable subgroup with greater functional limitation, worse metabolic and psychological health, and poorer survival. Burden-based stratification may better capture clinically meaningful heterogeneity than OA diagnosis alone.

title: Diagnostic value of multiparametric MRI radiomics combined with serum PSA and tissue P504S for prostate cancer.
abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic value of multiparametric MRI radiomics features combined with serum PSA-related indicators and tissue P504S expression for prostate cancer, and to develop a multimodal auxiliary diagnostic model in a retrospective cohort that was not restricted to early-stage disease. Clinical, imaging, and pathological data from 126 patients with suspected prostate cancer were retrospectively collected and divided into a prostate cancer group (69 cases) and a benign lesion group (57 cases). All patients underwent prostate MRI; radiomics features were extracted, and LASSO regression, with 10-fold cross-validation for tuning, was used to construct a Rad-score. Serum t-PSA, f-PSA, f/t-PSA ratio, and PSAD were measured. Tissue P504S expression was detected by immunohistochemistry and semi-quantitatively scored. A combined diagnostic model was constructed using multivariate logistic regression. ROC metrics were evaluated in the model-development cohort and are reported as apparent performance. AUC differences between models were compared using the DeLong test. The prostate cancer group had higher t-PSA and PSAD and a lower f/t-PSA ratio than the benign lesion group (all P < .001). P504S was positive in 64/69 cancer cases (92.8%) and 9/57 benign cases (15.8%; P < .001). Eight radiomics features were selected, and the median Rad-score was 0.86 in cancer cases and - 0.52 in benign cases (P < .001). The full model combining Rad-score, f/t-PSA, PSAD, and tissue P504S semiquantitative score achieved an apparent AUC of 0.956 (95% CI: 0.918-0.994), sensitivity of 92.8%, specificity of 91.2%, PPV of 92.8%, and NPV of 91.2%. The overall imaging + serum model had an apparent AUC of 0.912 (95% CI: 0.856-0.968). In exploratory location-based analyses, AUCs were 0.962 for peripheral zone lesions and 0.934 for transition zone lesions. The full model showed promising apparent discrimination for prostate cancer in this retrospective cohort and may represent a potential auxiliary diagnostic model after tissue sampling. The imaging + serum model could potentially support biopsy decision-making, whereas the full model requires tissue P504S assessment and may assist diagnostic confirmation or risk characterization. Neither incremental clinical benefit nor a reduction in unnecessary biopsies has been established. Internal and external validation and evaluation of the practical clinical workflow are required before routine use.

title: Prenatal clinical features and clinical outcomes of fetuses with 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 microdeletion syndrome: A single-center case series of 22 patients.
abstract: This study analyzes 22 fetuses with 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 microdeletion syndrome in Eastern China to investigate the prenatal clinical features and postnatal outcomes. We conducted a retrospective study of 22 fetuses diagnosed with 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 microdeletion (312-855 kilobase) via chromosomal microarray analysis among 2607 prenatal cases from January 2022 to September 2024. Parental origin, ultrasound findings, and postnatal outcomes were evaluated. The 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 microdeletion prevalence was 0.84% (22/2607). Prenatal ultrasound anomalies were observed in 54.5% (12/22), primarily mild cardiac findings (tricuspid regurgitation), choroid plexus cysts, and thickened nuchal translucency. Parental testing (13 cases) revealed 6 paternal, 6 maternal, and 1 de novo case. Postnatal follow-up of 18 live births (mean 14.7 months) showed normal development in most cases (17/18), with 1 child exhibiting delayed language development. Four pregnancies (18.2%) were terminated despite genetic counseling. Our study underscores that the 15q11.2 BP1-BP2 microdeletion exhibits incomplete penetrance and variable prenatal phenotypes, complicating outcome prediction. Long-term pediatric follow-up is essential, and early reassurance should be avoided even in cases with normal prenatal findings or favorable short-term outcomes.

title: Synchronous hepatocellular carcinoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma in a patient with chronic hepatitis B: A case report and literature review.
abstract: Rationale Synchronous double primary cancers involving hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) are exceptionally rare. Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection is an established cause of HCC, whereas Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection is the major etiological factor for NPC. We report a patient with synchronous HCC and NPC and review the relevant literature. Patient concerns A 63-year-old Chinese man with chronic HBV presented with a liver mass detected on routine screening. He reported nasal obstruction. Diagnoses Contrast-enhanced imaging showed a 46 × 59 mm hepatic lesion with portal vein tumor thrombus and a 41 × 29 mm nasopharyngeal mass with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Biopsies confirmed moderately differentiated HCC and EBV-associated non-keratinizing NPC. Final diagnoses were HCC Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer Stage C (CNLC IIIa, Child-Pugh A) and NPC T3N2M0 Stage III (AJCC 8th edition). Interventions He received hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy (HAIC, mFOLFOX) combined with tislelizumab and donafenib; radiotherapy for NPC was deferred after shared decision-making. Entecavir was continued. Outcomes At 19-month follow-up, both tumors remained controlled; the NPC met radiographic complete response criteria. Lessons Synchronous HCC and EBV-associated NPC were controlled during treatment with a tislelizumab-containing multimodality regimen, and the NPC achieved a radiographic complete response. The contribution of each treatment component cannot be determined from a single case, and definitive radiotherapy remains the standard of care for locoregionally advanced NPC. Multidisciplinary management and close monitoring are essential.

title: Successful rechallenge with almonertinib and corticosteroids after gefitinib-induced interstitial lung disease: A case report and literature review.
abstract: Rationale First-generation epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are highly effective in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC); however, drug-induced interstitial lung disease (ILD) remains a rare but potentially fatal adverse event. The safety and efficacy of EGFR-TKI rechallenge - either with the same agent or an alternative one - following ILD resolution are not established and represent a significant clinical knowledge gap. Patient concerns A 53-year-old never-smoking woman with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma - detected to harbor an L858R mutation in exon 21 of the EGFR gene - developed progressive dyspnea and hypoxemia after 2 months of first-line gefitinib therapy, despite confirmed initial radiographic and clinical response. Diagnoses The patient was diagnosed with grade 3 gefitinib-associated ILD. Interventions With the discontinuation of gefitinib, the patient was given methylprednisolone to resolve ILD. To control advanced lung adenocarcinoma progression, the patient was subjected to 6 cycles of treatment using pemetrexed, carboplatin, and bevacizumab, with measurable tumor shrinkage, followed by maintenance therapy with bevacizumab. Furthermore, given the tumor progression 14 months later, the patient was prescribed docetaxel plus bevacizumab to restore control. Ten months later, the patient experienced disease progression and strongly requested to use EGFR-TKIs again given prior response to EGFR-TKI. The patient was rechallenged with almonertinib, a third-generation EGFR-TKI, and methylprednisolone. Outcomes The patient had measurable tumor shrinkage, with sustained tumor control and no recurrence of pulmonary toxicity. As of last follow-up, she maintained progression-free survival for approximately 8 months on almonertinib. Lessons This case provides a hypothesis-generating observation, illustrating feasibility only in highly‑selected patients with EGFR‑mutant NSCLC and prior severe TKI‑related ILD. With prophylactic corticosteroids and rigorous surveillance, third‑generation EGFR‑TKI may represent a tentative clinical option for such patients, but general safety cannot be inferred from this single case.

title: Risk-adapted active surveillance for prostate cancer: Can mpMRI, biomarkers, and genomic classifiers reduce biopsy burden without compromising safety?: A systematic review.
abstract: Background Active surveillance is the preferred management strategy for men with low-risk and selected favorable intermediate-risk prostate cancer. However, conventional surveillance protocols rely heavily on repeated systematic biopsies, which impose procedural morbidity, patient burden, and limited precision in identifying true disease progression. Risk-adapted tools, including multi parametric magnetic resonance imaging (mpMRI), molecular biomarkers, and genomic classifiers, have emerged as potential strategies to optimize surveillance intensity while preserving oncologic safety. To systematically evaluate the evidence supporting risk-adapted AS strategies incorporating mpMRI, molecular biomarkers, and genomic classifiers, with a focus on reducing biopsy burden without compromising oncologic outcomes. Methods A systematic review was conducted in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus were searched for peer-reviewed studies evaluating mpMRI, molecular biomarkers, or genomic classifiers within AS cohorts. Randomized controlled trials and prospective or retrospective cohort studies reporting surveillance-related outcomes were included. Primary outcomes included biopsy upgrading or reclassification, AS failure, and oncologic safety endpoints. Due to methodological heterogeneity, results were synthesized narratively. Results Five publications met inclusion criteria, representing four unique studies one randomized controlled trial and three observational cohorts and 1215 participants. The 2 Active Surveillance Magnetic Resonance Imaging Study publications were treated as linked reports from the same trial. Baseline mpMRI with targeted and systematic biopsy was associated with lower subsequent AS failure and upgrading, but biopsy avoidance was not directly tested. An MRI-led cohort omitted routine protocol biopsies, although the absence of a concurrent comparator precluded conclusions about equivalent oncologic safety. The 4Kscore demonstrated potential for confirmatory-biopsy triage; a hypothetical deferral strategy could have avoided 27% of biopsies but would have missed 2 Grade Group 2 upgrades. The Decipher genomic classifier independently predicted biopsy upgrading, although biopsy reduction was not evaluated. Evidence establishing the long-term oncologic safety of biopsy reduction remained insufficient. Conclusion Risk-adapted AS strategies incorporating mpMRI, molecular biomarkers, and genomic classifiers may improve risk stratification and support selective adjustment of biopsy intensity. However, current evidence does not establish the safety of routine biopsy omission or fully biopsy-free surveillance. Integration of these tools should remain individualized, with histologic reassessment when indicated and prospective validation of biopsy-deferral strategies.

title: Lattice radiotherapy followed by chemoimmunotherapy for sustained disease control in bulky centrally located left hilar lung squamous cell carcinoma: A case report.
abstract: Rationale Bulky centrally located, locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer often abuts critical thoracic structures, making both upfront surgery and conventional radiotherapy dose escalation challenging. Lattice radiotherapy (LRT) may achieve tumor debulking while limiting radiation exposure to surrounding organs at risk. Patient concerns A 70-year-old man presented with a recurrent cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis for 6 months. Diagnoses Contrast-enhanced chest computed tomography revealed a 6.6 cm × 6.0 cm irregular left hilar mass with mediastinal invasion, encasement of the adjacent trachea and vessels, and an indistinct interface with the esophagus. Bronchoscopic biopsy confirmed squamous cell carcinoma of the lung. The programmed death-ligand 1 tumor proportion score was 18%. The final diagnosis was left hilar lung squamous cell carcinoma, cT4N1M0, stage IIIA. title: Adrenal ganglioneuroma in an adolescent presenting as an incidentaloma: Imaging-pathology correlation and diagnostic challenges: A case report.
abstract: Rationale Adrenal ganglioneuroma (AGN) is a rare, benign, and usually nonfunctioning tumor arising from neural crest-derived sympathetic ganglion cells. Preoperative diagnosis is difficult because the clinical presentation is often nonspecific, and imaging findings overlap with those of other adrenal neoplasms. We describe an adolescent adrenal incidentaloma with detailed imaging-pathology correlation, adding to the small number of reported adolescent cases. Patient concerns A previously healthy 16-year-old male underwent contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) after a bicycle accident. No traumatic injury was identified, but imaging incidentally revealed a well-circumscribed right adrenal mass measuring approximately 6.1 cm × 3.6 cm × 5.0 cm. Diagnoses CT and magnetic resonance imaging showed progressive, persistent enhancement across the arterial, venous, and delayed phases without demonstrable washout (attenuation increased from 20 Hounsfield units unenhanced to 55 Hounsfield units in the venous phase, with further qualitative enhancement on 15-minute delayed images) and no intralesional fat, suggesting a non-adenomatous lesion and raising suspicion for a neurogenic tumor. Biochemical evaluation showed no evidence of hormonal hypersecretion. Histopathological examination after resection established the diagnosis of AGN. Interventions The patient underwent right adrenalectomy because of the size and radiologically indeterminate nature of the mass. Outcomes The postoperative course was uneventful. Transient elevation of blood pressure noted during follow-up prompted biochemical reevaluation, which showed no evidence of excess catecholamine. Follow-up CT at 9 months showed no recurrence. Lessons Progressive delayed enhancement without washout and absence of signal loss on opposed-phase magnetic resonance imaging, a pattern previously described in ganglioneuroma, may suggest the diagnosis preoperatively, although definitive diagnosis requires histopathological confirmation. Complete surgical excision established the diagnosis and achieved a favorable short-term outcome; the excellent long-term prognosis of AGN is supported by the published literature, and our patient remains recurrence-free at 9 months.

title: Metastatic G2 laryngeal neuroendocrine tumor treated with sulfatinib and sintilimab: A case report and literature review.
abstract: Rationale Laryngeal neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) are rare and heterogeneous malignancies with limited evidence guiding the management of metastatic disease. We report a metastatic G2 laryngeal NET initially presenting as an unusual temporal subcutaneous metastasis and subsequently treated with combined targeted therapy and immunotherapy. Patient concerns A 63-year-old man with a history of invasive lung adenocarcinoma presented with a 1.3 × 1.2 cm left temporal subcutaneous nodule and a history of hoarseness accompanied by throat pain. Diagnoses Histopathological examination of the temporal lesion suggested metastatic NET. Subsequent PET-CT, laryngoscopy, and biopsy identified a primary laryngeal NET. After vertical partial laryngectomy, right neck dissection, and laryngeal function reconstruction, pathology confirmed a well-differentiated G2 NET with cervical lymph-node and temporal subcutaneous metastases, classified as pT2N1M1, stage IVC. In March 2025, hepatic metastases were pathologically confirmed. Molecular profiling identified HRAS p.Q61L, KDR p.S265L, and ROS1 p.S615Y variants, microsatellite instability-high status, and programmed death-ligand 1expression with a combined positive score of 70. Interventions Combination therapy with sulfatinib (300 mg/day) and sintilimab (200 mg every 3 weeks) was initiated in April 2025 and continued without dose reduction, interruption, or delay. Outcomes After 10 months of combination therapy, contrast-enhanced CT demonstrated a reduction in the size of hepatic metastatic lesions compared with baseline, together with a marked decrease in the number of metastatic lesions. The largest index hepatic lesion decreased from 32.68 mm to 19.05 mm in maximal diameter, corresponding to a 41.7% reduction, demonstrating a marked radiological reduction in hepatic metastatic burden. At the latest documented assessment in February 2026, no further disease progression or treatment-related adverse events were observed. Lessons This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of metastatic laryngeal NET with an unusual subcutaneous presentation. Comprehensive pathological and molecular evaluation may aid treatment decision-making in advanced disease. The observed disease control with sulfatinib plus sintilimab is hypothesis-generating and requires validation in additional patients.
